lessons.title: Lesson 1: Discovering God's Original Purpose for Human Existence
lessons.theme: Discovering God's original purpose for human existence
lessons.memoryVerse: "Even every one that is called by my name: for I have created him for my glory, I have formed him; yea, I have made him." — Isaiah 43:7 (KJV)
lessons.introduction:
One of the greatest questions confronting humanity is not simply, "What do I want to become?" but "Why am I here?"

People spend years pursuing education, acquiring wealth, building careers, establishing businesses, raising families, seeking recognition and struggling to achieve personal ambitions. Yet, despite these accomplishments, many still experience an uncomfortable emptiness because they have not discovered the deeper reason for their existence.

A person can become highly educated and still lack direction. Someone can become wealthy and remain unfulfilled. Another can occupy an influential position and still struggle with a sense of worthlessness. It is possible to achieve everything society celebrates and yet fail to fulfil the purpose for which God created you.

The problem is that many people are pursuing success without first understanding purpose.

Consider a manufacturer who produces a machine. The machine's purpose is determined by its manufacturer, not by the machine itself. If the machine abandons its intended function and begins operating according to its own assumptions, it may become useless despite being expensive and beautifully designed.

In the same way, human beings cannot fully understand the meaning of existence independently of their Creator.

God did not create humanity merely to eat, sleep, reproduce, acquire possessions and eventually die. He created us with divine intention, moral responsibility, relational capacity and an assignment within His creation.

However, understanding this purpose requires more than attending church or becoming religious. It requires discovering God's intention and allowing that intention to govern the way we live.

Consider this question:

If all your possessions, qualifications, titles, achievements and public recognition were taken away today, would you still understand why God created you and what makes your life meaningful?

That is where the journey towards understanding divine purpose begins.
lessonObjectives: KNOW: Understand God's original intention for creating humanity, the meaning of human existence and the relationship between divine purpose and human responsibility.
BELIEVE: Believe that human life is neither accidental nor meaningless, but a divine gift entrusted to humanity for God's glory and the fulfilment of His purposes.
PRACTICE: Begin to organise personal decisions, relationships, talents, resources and daily activities around God's purpose rather than selfish ambition, societal pressure or temporary pleasures.

lessons.lessonContent:
A. BIBLICAL EXPLANATION (WHAT THE TEXT MEANS)

1. Genesis 1:26–28 – Humanity Was Created in God's Image and Likeness

"And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness..." (Genesis 1:26, KJV).

The creation of humanity was different from the creation of other creatures. God deliberately introduced humanity as the bearer of His image and likeness.

This reveals several important truths.

a. Humanity has inherent dignity and value.

Human worth is not determined by educational qualifications, financial capacity, physical appearance, social class, ethnicity, gender, occupation or public recognition.

A poor person has the same fundamental human dignity as a wealthy person. An educated person is not more valuable before God than an uneducated person.

This truth should influence how Christians treat domestic workers, children, elderly people, prisoners, refugees, persons with disabilities and people from different backgrounds.

Nobody should be treated as disposable because every human being possesses dignity as God's image-bearer.

b. Humanity was created for relationship.

The image of God points to humanity's capacity for relationship, moral responsibility, love, communication and fellowship.

God created us to know Him, relate with others and live responsibly within His creation.

This explains why isolation, selfishness, hatred and destructive relationships contradict God's intention for human life.

c. Humanity received responsibility and authority.

Genesis 1:28 introduces the responsibility of fruitfulness, multiplication, filling the earth and exercising dominion.

Dominion does not mean permission to destroy, exploit or abuse creation. It means responsible stewardship under God's authority.

Human beings were created to manage resources, develop their environment, cultivate productive activities and exercise authority responsibly.

A Christian who steals public resources, destroys the environment, exploits workers or abuses people in authority has misunderstood the biblical meaning of dominion.

Important lesson: We were created with dignity, relationship and responsibility. These three dimensions must remain connected.

2. Isaiah 43:7 – Humanity Was Created for God's Glory

God declares that He created His people for His glory.

What does it mean to live for God's glory?

It means living in such a way that our existence, conduct, choices and achievements reflect God's character and honour His name.

God's glory is not limited to singing in church, preaching, fasting or participating in religious programmes.

A teacher glorifies God by teaching honestly and diligently. A business owner glorifies God by refusing to deceive customers. A parent glorifies God by raising children with love, discipline and godly values.

A civil servant glorifies God by rejecting bribery. A student glorifies God by studying honestly. A Christian professional glorifies God through excellence and integrity.

In Matthew 5:16, Jesus teaches that people should see our good works and glorify our Father in heaven.

Therefore, God's glory should be visible in the ordinary activities of life.

A major mistake Christians make is separating spiritual life from everyday responsibilities. Some people are careful about their conduct in church but careless about their conduct in business, marriage, employment and personal relationships.

Yet God's purpose covers the whole of human existence.

3. Ephesians 2:10 – We Were Created for Good Works

"For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works..." (Ephesians 2:10, KJV).

This scripture introduces an important dimension of divine purpose: purposeful living involves meaningful contribution.

Notice that Paul first explains salvation by grace through faith in Ephesians 2:8–9. He then explains in verse 10 that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.

This means good works are not the price we pay to obtain salvation; they are the fruit and expression of a life transformed by salvation.

God has prepared opportunities for His children to demonstrate His goodness through their lives.

These good works include:

* Helping people in need.
* Raising responsible children.
* Supporting the weak and vulnerable.
* Promoting justice and fairness.
* Developing useful skills.
* Serving faithfully in the Church.
* Contributing to community development.
* Sharing the gospel.
* Using professional abilities to solve problems.
* Demonstrating love, compassion and integrity.

Consider the story of Dorcas in Acts 9:36–39. She was known for good works and acts of charity. Her life made a meaningful difference to widows and vulnerable people in her community.

She may not have occupied a prominent political or religious office, but her contribution was significant.

This teaches us that fulfilling purpose is not necessarily about occupying a famous position. It is about faithfully fulfilling God's assignment with the opportunities and abilities He has entrusted to us.

4. Colossians 1:15–17 – Christ Is the Centre of Human Existence

"For by him were all things created..." (Colossians 1:16, KJV).

Paul presents Christ as the centre of creation. All things were created by Him and for Him.

This is foundational to understanding human purpose.

Christianity does not teach that human beings are the centre of the universe. God is the centre, and Jesus Christ is Lord over creation.

Therefore, purpose must be understood in relationship with Christ.

When people make money, personal ambition, relationships, pleasure, political power or professional success the centre of their existence, they place created things above the Creator.

Even good things can become destructive when they occupy the position that belongs to God.

Marriage is good, but marriage cannot replace God. Wealth is useful, but wealth cannot become one's god. Education is valuable, but intellectual achievement cannot replace obedience to Christ.

A purposeful Christian life begins with Christ, is sustained by Christ and ultimately points back to Christ.

5. Revelation 4:11 – We Exist Because of God's Will and Pleasure

"Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created." (Revelation 4:11, KJV).

This passage reminds us that creation exists because of God's sovereign will.

Human existence is not self-originated. We did not create ourselves, determine our original existence or establish the conditions under which we entered the world.

Life is a gift from God.

Consequently, we are accountable to the One who gave us life.

This should change our attitude towards time, opportunities, relationships, resources and responsibilities.

The question should no longer be merely, "What can I get from life?" but also, "What does God expect me to do with the life He has given me?"

B. THEOLOGICAL CLARIFICATION (AVOIDING EXTREMES)

Understanding divine purpose requires biblical balance. Several misconceptions must be corrected.

1. Purpose versus Personal Ambition

Personal ambition is not necessarily sinful. It is good to desire education, professional excellence, financial stability, business growth and meaningful achievements.

However, personal ambition must be submitted to God's authority.

James 4:13–16 warns against making plans without acknowledging God's sovereignty.

The problem is not planning for the future; the problem is planning as though God has no authority over our lives.

2. Purpose versus Position

Not everyone will become a pastor, bishop, politician, professor, business magnate or internationally recognised personality.

God's purpose is not measured by public visibility.

Joseph served faithfully in prison before becoming governor. David served as a shepherd before becoming king. Dorcas served vulnerable people without occupying a prominent public office.

Never despise a meaningful assignment because it does not attract public recognition.

3. Purpose versus Wealth and Prosperity

God can bless people with wealth, but wealth is not the universal evidence of divine approval.

Some faithful believers experience financial hardship, persecution and difficult circumstances.

The biblical measure of a purposeful life is faithfulness to God, not the size of one's bank account.

See Luke 12:15 and 1 Timothy 6:6–10.

4. Divine Purpose versus Human Irresponsibility

Some people claim to be waiting for God's purpose while refusing to work, study, develop skills or take responsibility.

This is not biblical spirituality.

Proverbs 6:6–11 teaches diligence, while Ecclesiastes 9:10 encourages people to work with commitment.

Trusting God does not excuse laziness.

5. God's Sovereignty versus Human Responsibility

God is sovereign, but human beings are responsible for their decisions.

The existence of divine purpose does not mean every decision we make is automatically God's will.

We must exercise wisdom, seek godly counsel, study Scripture and accept responsibility for our choices.

C. DOCTRINAL ALIGNMENT

The following biblical doctrines help establish a sound understanding of human purpose.

1. The Doctrine of Creation

God is the Creator of humanity. Human existence originates from His will and not from human self-determination (Genesis 1:26–27).

2. The Doctrine of the Image of God (Imago Dei)

Every human being possesses inherent dignity and value. This establishes the biblical foundation for human respect, compassion, justice and responsible treatment of others.

3. The Doctrine of Stewardship

Human beings are entrusted with life, time, talents, relationships, resources and the environment. These are responsibilities to be managed faithfully (Genesis 2:15; Matthew 25:14–30).

4. The Doctrine of Salvation and Transformation

Sin disrupted humanity's relationship with God, but salvation through Jesus Christ restores fellowship with God and establishes a new life of obedience and good works (Ephesians 2:1–10).

5. The Doctrine of Glorification and Eternal Accountability

Human life must be understood in the light of eternity. Every person will ultimately give an account before God (Romans 14:10–12; 2 Corinthians 5:10).

D. KEY TRUTHS / LESSON HIGHLIGHTS

* You were created by God, and your existence has divine significance.
* Human worth is established by God's creation, not by society's measurements.
* God's purpose involves knowing Him, reflecting His character and serving His creation.
* Your occupation is an avenue for expressing purpose, not necessarily the totality of your purpose.
* Spirituality must influence your family, workplace, business and community life.
* Wealth, popularity and position cannot replace a meaningful relationship with God.
* Every believer has opportunities to perform good works.
* Purpose is not discovered through selfish ambition but through relationship with God and obedience to His Word.
* You are a steward of the life God has entrusted to you.
* A meaningful life is one that honours God and positively impacts others.

E. LIFE APPLICATION

The purpose of this lesson is not simply to make participants understand creation intellectually. It is to help them examine how they are living.

1. Examine Your Priorities

Look at how you spend your time, money, energy and attention.

Are your daily activities consistent with your Christian convictions?

A person who spends several hours on entertainment but cannot devote a few minutes to prayer, Scripture or meaningful family interaction should reconsider their priorities.

2. Discover Your Areas of Responsibility

God has entrusted every person with certain responsibilities.

You may be a parent, student, entrepreneur, teacher, pastor, civil servant, farmer, professional or community leader.

Ask yourself: How can I honour God through this responsibility?

Do not wait for a religious title before becoming useful to God.

3. Identify Your God-Given Abilities

What abilities, experiences, knowledge and opportunities has God placed in your hands?

You may be good at teaching, organising, counselling, administration, agriculture, technology, communication, hospitality or problem-solving.

Develop these abilities and use them responsibly to serve God and humanity.

4. Reconsider Your Definition of Success

Success should not be measured only by the house you own, the car you drive, your academic certificates or your social status.

A person who gains wealth but destroys their family, sacrifices integrity and abandons God has misunderstood success.

5. Become a Blessing to Someone

Identify one person or group you can positively influence this week.

It could be a struggling student, a neglected elderly person, a struggling family, a young person facing peer pressure or someone in need of encouragement.

Purpose becomes practical when it produces positive impact.

G. CASE STUDY / REAL-LIFE SCENARIO

Case Study: The Successful but Unfulfilled Businessman

A 42-year-old businessman has established several successful businesses. He owns properties, drives expensive vehicles, travels internationally and is respected within his professional circle.

However, he rarely spends time with his family. His children have little meaningful relationship with him. He is dishonest in some business dealings, regularly compromises his Christian convictions to secure contracts and has gradually abandoned his personal relationship with God.

Whenever someone challenges his lifestyle, he responds:

"I am working hard to secure my future. Once I have made enough money, I will have time for God and my family."

Unfortunately, several years have passed, and his definition of enough keeps changing.

Questions for Discussion:

* Is this man successful? Explain your answer from a biblical perspective.
* What has he misunderstood about the purpose of wealth and professional achievement?
* What dangers arise when people continually postpone their spiritual and family responsibilities?
* How can he reorganise his life without necessarily abandoning his business?
* What lessons can young Christians learn from this situation?

Biblical Reference: Mark 8:36; Luke 12:16–21; 1 Timothy 6:17–19.

Teaching Lesson: It is possible to gain the whole world and gradually lose what matters most. God does not necessarily condemn wealth or achievement, but He condemns misplaced priorities and unfaithful stewardship.

H. PERSONAL REFLECTION AND SPIRITUAL EXAMINATION

Take a quiet moment and answer these questions honestly before God.

* Do I understand why God created me?
* Have I allowed society's definition of success to replace God's purpose for my life?
* Am I using my talents, education, financial resources and opportunities responsibly?
* Does my private life reflect the Christian values I profess publicly?
* Are the people around me experiencing God's goodness through my life?
* If I were to stand before God today, what would my life say about the way I used the opportunities He gave me?

Personal Declaration:

I am not an accident. God created me with dignity, purpose and responsibility. I will not waste my life pursuing things that have no eternal value. My talents, time, resources, relationships and opportunities will be submitted to God's will. Through Christ, I will live a life that honours God and positively impacts humanity.

I. ACTION POINT FOR THE WEEK

MY PURPOSE DISCOVERY ASSIGNMENT

During this week, complete the following five exercises:

WEEKLY PROGRESS

0/5

* Write down five reasons you believe God created you, using biblical references.
* Identify three abilities or resources God has entrusted to you.
* Identify two areas of your life where your priorities need correction.
* Choose one practical way to make a positive difference in someone's life this week.
* Spend at least 20 minutes reflecting and praying about how to align your daily activities with God's purpose.

Declaration for the Week:

"My life has divine significance. I was created for God's glory. I will not live carelessly, compete unnecessarily or measure my worth by worldly standards. I will discover, develop and faithfully fulfil my God-given responsibilities. My life will be a blessing to my generation, and my existence will bring glory to God. In Jesus' name. Amen."

J. CLOSING PRAYER

* Father, thank You for the gift of life and for creating me with divine intention.
* Lord, deliver me from living a purposeless life and pursuing things that distract me from Your will.
* Open my understanding to recognise the gifts, abilities and opportunities You have entrusted to me.
* Give me wisdom to use my time, resources, relationships and abilities responsibly.
* Help me to become a blessing to my family, Church, community and generation.
* Let my life bring glory to Your name, in Jesus' mighty name. Amen.

lessons.conclusion:
The greatest tragedy is not necessarily dying without acquiring wealth, occupying a prominent position or becoming famous. A greater tragedy is living without understanding why God gave us life and failing to use the opportunities He entrusted to us.

God created humanity with dignity, purpose and responsibility. Through Jesus Christ, we are called into a restored relationship with our Creator and commissioned to live lives that reflect His character.

Therefore, do not spend your entire life trying to become somebody in the eyes of the world while neglecting the person God wants you to become.

You were created by God, you exist through His sustaining grace, and your life should ultimately bring glory to Him.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The New Birth – The Beginning of a New Life in Christ
lessons.theme: The new birth and the beginning of a new life in Christ
lessons.memoryVerse: "Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." — John 3:3 (KJV)
lessons.introduction:
One of the greatest mistakes people make about Christianity is assuming that being religious is the same thing as being born again.

Some people grew up in Christian homes. They attended Sunday School as children, participated in church activities, memorised Bible verses, joined choirs, served in religious departments and became familiar with Christian language. Yet, familiarity with Christianity does not automatically mean that a person has experienced salvation.

A person can be born into a Christian family without being born again. Someone can occupy a position in the Church without experiencing genuine spiritual transformation. Another person can know several Bible passages but remain controlled by sinful habits, selfishness and rebellion against God.

Christianity is not fundamentally about changing one's religious association; it is about experiencing a new life through Jesus Christ.

Consider a person who owns an old building with serious structural defects. The owner paints the walls, changes the curtains, installs new furniture and decorates the rooms. Although the building looks different externally, the underlying structural problems remain.

What is needed is not merely external decoration but fundamental restoration.

In the same way, human beings do not simply need moral decoration. We need spiritual regeneration.

This was the central issue Jesus addressed when Nicodemus, a respected religious leader, visited Him at night.

Nicodemus possessed religious knowledge, social recognition and moral respectability. Yet Jesus told him that he needed to be born again.

This reveals an important truth: religious knowledge cannot replace spiritual regeneration.

The new birth is the beginning of the Christian life. It is the foundation upon which spiritual growth, godly character, Christian service and eternal hope are built.

Have you genuinely experienced the new birth, or have you simply become familiar with the activities and language of Christianity?
lessonObjectives: KNOW: Understand the biblical meaning of the new birth, why every human being needs salvation, and the difference between religious activities and genuine spiritual regeneration.
BELIEVE: Believe that salvation is God's gracious provision through Jesus Christ and that genuine conversion produces a new spiritual identity and a transformed relationship with God.
PRACTICE: Demonstrate evidence of the new birth through repentance, faith in Christ, obedience to God's Word, transformed character and a consistent Christian lifestyle.

lessons.lessonContent:
A. BIBLICAL EXPLANATION (WHAT THE TEXT MEANS)

1. John 3:1–8 – The New Birth Is a Spiritual Necessity

The encounter between Jesus and Nicodemus provides one of the clearest biblical explanations of the new birth.

Nicodemus was a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews. He was educated in religious matters, familiar with the Jewish Scriptures and respected within his community.

He approached Jesus and acknowledged that His ministry demonstrated divine authority.

However, Jesus immediately addressed a deeper issue.

"Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." (John 3:3).

Why did Jesus make such a statement to someone who was already religious?

Because religious knowledge and spiritual regeneration are two different things.

a. The new birth is not physical rebirth.

Nicodemus initially misunderstood Jesus' statement. He wondered how an adult could return to his mother's womb and be born again.

Jesus explained that He was speaking about spiritual birth.

The new birth is not a physical experience or a second biological birth. It is the work of the Holy Spirit through which a person receives new spiritual life.

b. The new birth is the work of the Holy Spirit.

Jesus explained:

"That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit." (John 3:6).

Human effort cannot produce spiritual regeneration.

Education can improve intellectual understanding. Discipline can improve behaviour. Social development can improve interpersonal relationships. Religious training can increase biblical knowledge.

However, none of these independently gives a person new spiritual life.

The Holy Spirit is the agent of regeneration.

c. The new birth is available to everyone.

Jesus did not tell Nicodemus that only certain categories of people needed the new birth.

The requirement applies to everyone.

Whether someone is rich or poor, educated or uneducated, young or elderly, a church worker or a first-time visitor, everyone needs salvation through Christ.

The new birth is not an optional spiritual upgrade. It is essential to entering God's Kingdom.

2. Titus 3:3–7 – Salvation Is Based on God's Mercy, Not Human Achievement

Paul gives an important explanation of salvation in his letter to Titus.

He describes humanity's former condition and then explains what God accomplished through His mercy.

Verse 5 states:

"Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost."

This passage establishes several foundational truths.

a. Humanity needs spiritual restoration.

Paul describes the former human condition through disobedience, deception, uncontrolled desires, malice, envy and hatred.

This is a picture of humanity affected by sin.

Sin is not merely a collection of bad habits. It is a condition of rebellion against God that affects human desires, decisions, relationships and conduct.

b. Salvation originates from God's mercy.

God did not save us because we were sufficiently good, intelligent, wealthy or religious.

He saved us because of His mercy.

This removes every ground for spiritual pride.

No Christian should look down on another person as though salvation were a personal achievement.

c. Regeneration involves spiritual renewal.

The washing of regeneration describes God's cleansing and renewal of the sinner.

Through the Holy Spirit, God brings about a new spiritual beginning.

This does not mean that every believer immediately becomes perfect or stops experiencing temptation. It means that a new relationship with God has begun and a new direction of life has been established.

d. Salvation brings a new standing before God.

Titus 3:7 connects salvation with justification by grace and the hope of eternal life.

The believer is not merely trying to become a better person; the believer has received a new standing before God through Christ.

3. 2 Corinthians 5:17 – The New Birth Produces a New Identity

"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."

This scripture is one of the clearest descriptions of the transformation that takes place in Christ.

Notice the expression, "in Christ."

The foundation of the new identity is not membership in a denomination, attendance at religious programmes or association with Christian leaders.

It is a personal relationship with Jesus Christ.

a. A new spiritual identity

The believer is no longer defined primarily by the former life of sin.

Past failures, destructive habits and previous patterns of rebellion do not have to determine the person's future.

In Christ, there is a new identity.

b. A new relationship with sin

The new birth changes a person's attitude towards sin.

Before conversion, someone may defend, celebrate or deliberately practise sinful behaviour without concern.

After genuine conversion, the believer develops a new desire to please God.

There may still be struggles, but sin is no longer supposed to be accepted as a permanent lifestyle.

c. A new orientation towards life

The believer begins to see life differently.

Decisions are evaluated through biblical principles. Relationships are reconsidered. Priorities change. The desire to know God increases.

A person who previously enjoyed dishonesty may begin to value integrity. Someone who lived for personal pleasure may develop compassion for others.

This is the evidence of a life being transformed.

Important clarification: Becoming a new creature does not mean forgetting every memory of the past or immediately losing every weakness. It means receiving a new identity and beginning a transformed life under Christ's authority.

4. Romans 6:1–14 – The New Birth Changes Our Relationship with Sin

Paul raises an important question:

"Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?" (Romans 6:1).

His answer is emphatic:

"God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?" (Romans 6:2).

Paul is correcting the idea that salvation gives people permission to continue living in sin.

a. Believers are united with Christ in His death and resurrection.

Romans 6 explains that through faith, believers are identified with Christ's death and resurrection.

His death represents the decisive break with the dominion of sin, while His resurrection establishes the foundation of new life.

b. Sin must no longer exercise dominion.

Verse 12 says:

"Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that ye should obey it in the lusts thereof."

This means Christians must take responsibility for their conduct.

A believer cannot deliberately continue practising dishonesty, sexual immorality, hatred, corruption or destructive behaviour and use grace as an excuse.

c. The believer must present himself to God.

Romans 6:13 teaches that believers should present themselves to God as instruments of righteousness.

Our bodies, abilities, resources and decisions should become instruments for God's purposes.

The Christian life therefore involves deliberate obedience.

5. Ephesians 2:1–10 – From Spiritual Death to Life in Christ

Paul describes the former condition of humanity as being spiritually dead in trespasses and sins.

This does not mean people were physically dead or incapable of performing ordinary human activities. It describes separation from the life of God and bondage to sin.

But verses 4 and 5 introduce the wonderful intervention of divine mercy:

"But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us..."

God made us alive together with Christ.

This passage teaches four important lessons:

* Our former condition: Humanity is affected by sin and cannot independently restore its relationship with God.
* God's intervention: Salvation begins with God's love, mercy and grace.
* The means of salvation: We are saved by grace through faith, not by our own works.
* The result of salvation: We become God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.

The new birth is therefore not merely an emotional experience during a church service. It is a spiritual transition that establishes a new relationship with God and a new responsibility to live righteously.

B. THEOLOGICAL CLARIFICATION (AVOIDING EXTREMES)

Several misconceptions about the new birth must be addressed to preserve sound biblical understanding.

1. New Birth versus Church Membership

Church membership is valuable because believers need fellowship, teaching, accountability and spiritual growth.

However, membership in a local church does not automatically guarantee salvation.

A person may be registered in a church for decades without personally surrendering to Christ.

The new birth is a personal spiritual experience through faith in Jesus Christ.

See John 1:12–13.

2. New Birth versus Moral Reformation

Moral reformation means changing certain behaviours.

For example, a person may stop drinking, become more disciplined, improve their language and begin treating people more respectfully.

These are positive changes, but behavioural improvement alone does not constitute regeneration.

The new birth is God's work within the person, producing a new spiritual life that increasingly influences outward conduct.

3. Grace versus Permission to Continue in Sin

Some people misunderstand grace as permission to live carelessly.

Biblical grace does not encourage rebellion against God.

Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to reject ungodliness and worldly desires and to live soberly, righteously and godly.

Grace does not make holiness unnecessary. It empowers and trains believers towards holy living.

4. Conversion versus Instant Spiritual Maturity

A person may genuinely become born again without immediately possessing mature Christian character.

The new birth begins the Christian journey; discipleship develops the believer.

A new convert needs biblical instruction, fellowship, spiritual discipline, mentoring and opportunities to practise Christian living.

Do not confuse spiritual infancy with spiritual failure. However, believers must not use spiritual infancy as an excuse for refusing to grow.

5. Assurance of Salvation versus Presumption

Some people claim salvation merely because they once attended an altar call or repeated a prayer.

A sincere response to the gospel is important, but biblical assurance rests on God's promises in Christ and is accompanied by a growing life of faith and obedience.

1 John 5:11–13 teaches that eternal life is in God's Son.

At the same time, 1 John 2:3–6 emphasises the importance of obedience as evidence of knowing Christ.

We must avoid both extremes: living in unnecessary fear that God cannot save us, and living carelessly while claiming salvation without regard for Christ's authority.

C. DOCTRINAL ALIGNMENT

1. The Doctrine of Sin

All human beings have sinned and need God's salvation. No individual can establish righteousness before God through personal merit.

Scriptures: Romans 3:10–23; Romans 5:12.

2. The Doctrine of Salvation by Grace

Salvation is God's gracious provision, received through faith in Jesus Christ. Human works cannot purchase it.

Scriptures: Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 5:1–2.

3. The Doctrine of Regeneration

Regeneration is the spiritual work of the Holy Spirit through which a person receives new spiritual life.

Scriptures: John 3:5–8; Titus 3:5.

4. The Doctrine of Justification

Through faith in Christ, the believer is declared righteous before God. This is not a reward for personal achievement but an act of God's grace.

Scriptures: Romans 3:24–26; Romans 5:1.

5. The Doctrine of Sanctification

The believer is called to grow in holiness and become increasingly conformed to the character of Christ.

Scriptures: 1 Thessalonians 4:3–7; 2 Corinthians 3:18.

6. The Doctrine of Perseverance and Eternal Life

The Christian life is a continuing journey of faith in Christ. Believers are called to remain in Him, grow in obedience and hold firmly to the hope of eternal life.

Scriptures: John 15:4–6; Hebrews 3:12–14; 1 John 5:11–13.

D. KEY TRUTHS / LESSON HIGHLIGHTS

* Being born into a Christian family does not automatically make someone a Christian.
* Church attendance and religious activities cannot replace personal salvation.
* Every human being needs the new birth because sin has affected humanity.
* The Holy Spirit is the agent of spiritual regeneration.
* Salvation is received through God's grace by faith in Jesus Christ.
* The new birth establishes a new identity and relationship with God.
* Genuine conversion produces a new attitude towards sin.
* Grace is not permission to continue living in rebellion against God.
* Spiritual maturity develops through discipleship and obedience.
* A transformed life should increasingly reflect the character of Jesus Christ.

E. LIFE APPLICATION

The new birth must become visible in everyday Christian living.

1. Examine the Foundation of Your Faith

Do not assume that you are saved simply because you grew up in church.

Ask yourself whether you have personally acknowledged your sin, repented and placed your faith in Jesus Christ.

Christianity must move from family tradition to personal conviction.

2. Develop a New Relationship with God's Word

A newborn Christian needs spiritual nourishment.

Just as a physical baby requires food for growth, a new believer needs the Word of God.

Develop a regular Bible-reading habit. Study passages in context, ask questions, seek understanding and practise what you learn.

See 1 Peter 2:2.

3. Identify and Confront Destructive Habits

Examine areas of your life that contradict your Christian confession.

These may include:

* Dishonesty and financial misconduct.
* Sexual immorality and pornography.
* Unforgiveness and bitterness.
* Gossip and destructive speech.
* Alcohol or substance abuse.
* Uncontrolled anger.
* Pride and selfishness.
* Manipulation and exploitation.
* Unhealthy relationships.

Seek biblical counsel, accountability and appropriate professional support where needed.

Do not normalise what God calls you to overcome.

4. Change Your Relationship with People

A genuine encounter with Christ should influence how you treat people.

If you were dishonest before conversion, practise honesty. If you were abusive, learn to treat people with respect. If you exploited others, make restitution where appropriate and possible.

Consider Zacchaeus in Luke 19:1–10. His encounter with Jesus produced practical changes in his relationship with money and people he had wronged.

5. Join a Healthy Discipleship Community

New believers need support.

Find a Bible-believing local church where Scripture is taught responsibly and where you can receive guidance, fellowship and accountability.

Do not attempt to grow entirely in isolation.

6. Become an Example of Transformation

Your family, colleagues, neighbours and friends should gradually observe the difference Christ is making in your life.

You do not need to announce your conversion every day. Your conduct should increasingly provide evidence of your changed priorities.

G. CASE STUDY / REAL-LIFE SCENARIO

Case Study: The Church Worker Who Has Never Experienced Personal Conversion

A 35-year-old man has been attending church since childhood. His parents were committed Christians, and he has served in several church departments.

He is currently a departmental leader. He knows many Bible verses and regularly participates in church activities.

However, outside the Church, he is involved in fraudulent business practices. He regularly lies to customers, maintains secret immoral relationships and uses his position to intimidate younger members who disagree with him.

When challenged about his conduct, he responds:

"Nobody is perfect. I have been in church all my life. God understands me. Besides, we are saved by grace, not by works."

Recently, during a Sunday School lesson on the new birth, he begins to question whether he has ever genuinely surrendered his life to Christ.

Questions for Discussion:

* What is the difference between this man's religious experience and genuine conversion?
* Does his church position establish that he has experienced the new birth?
* Is he correctly applying the biblical doctrine of salvation by grace?
* What steps should he take if he recognises that his lifestyle contradicts the gospel?
* How should the Church address such situations without encouraging hypocrisy or treating people without compassion?
* What does this case teach us about the relationship between salvation and transformed living?

Biblical References: John 3:1–8; Matthew 7:21–23; Titus 2:11–14; 1 John 2:3–6.

Teaching Lesson:

Religious position is not a substitute for spiritual life. The Church must never allow titles, family background, length of membership or public activities to become substitutes for genuine conversion.

At the same time, the purpose of correction is restoration, not humiliation.

A person who discovers that their spiritual foundation is wrong should be encouraged to respond to Christ genuinely.

H. PERSONAL REFLECTION AND SPIRITUAL EXAMINATION

Take time to examine your spiritual life honestly before God.

* Have I personally surrendered my life to Jesus Christ?
* Am I relying on my Christian family background or church activities as evidence of salvation?
* Is there a genuine change in my attitude towards sin?
* Am I willing to obey Christ even when obedience is inconvenient?
* Are there areas of my life where I use grace as an excuse for deliberate disobedience?
* Am I growing spiritually, or have I remained at the same level of Christian understanding for years?
* If someone examined my private life, would they find evidence of my commitment to Christ?

A Moment of Personal Prayer

Lord Jesus, I acknowledge that I need You. I do not want to substitute religious activities for a genuine relationship with You. Search my heart, expose every area of hypocrisy and rebellion, and help me surrender completely to Your lordship. Let Your Spirit renew my heart and establish my life in Your truth. Amen.

I. INVITATION TO SALVATION AND PRAYER OF COMMITMENT

This section is especially important for Sunday School teachers to use when teaching participants who may not have personally received Christ.

The new birth begins with a response to the gospel.

Step 1: Acknowledge your need for salvation.

Recognise that you have sinned and cannot save yourself through personal achievements or religious activities.

Romans 3:23.

Step 2: Believe in Jesus Christ.

Believe that Jesus Christ died for our sins and rose again. He is the only Saviour and the foundation of our reconciliation with God.

Romans 10:9–10.

Step 3: Repent of your sins.

Repentance involves a change of mind and direction concerning sin and a willingness to turn towards God.

Acts 3:19.

Step 4: Receive Christ and surrender to His lordship.

Trust in Christ personally, not merely as a historical figure or religious teacher, but as Saviour and Lord.

John 1:12.

Suggested Prayer of Commitment

Heavenly Father, I come before You in the name of Jesus Christ.

I acknowledge that I am a sinner and that I cannot save myself through my own efforts, goodness or religious activities.

I believe that Jesus Christ died for my sins and rose again from the dead.

Today, I repent of my sins and place my faith in Jesus Christ as my Lord and Saviour.

Forgive me, cleanse me and give me new life through Your Holy Spirit.

I surrender my heart, my decisions, my relationships and my future to Your authority.

Help me to grow in Your Word, overcome sin, develop godly character and live a life that brings glory to Your name.

Thank You for Your mercy and the gift of salvation.

In Jesus' name. Amen.

Note to the teacher: This prayer is a guide, not a magical formula. Emphasise that salvation comes through genuine repentance and personal faith in Jesus Christ.

J. ACTION POINT FOR THE WEEK

MY NEW LIFE IN CHRIST – WEEKLY ASSIGNMENT

Complete these five exercises during the week.

WEEKLY PROGRESS

0/5

* Read John 3:1–8 and write down three things Jesus taught Nicodemus about the new birth.
* Read 2 Corinthians 5:17 and identify three areas where your attitude or conduct needs transformation.
* Identify one destructive habit or sinful pattern that you need to confront and take a practical step towards overcoming it.
* Establish a daily Bible-reading and prayer routine for at least 15–20 minutes.
* Encourage or support one person who needs help understanding the gospel and growing in Christ.

Declaration for the Week:

"I am a new creation in Christ Jesus. My past does not determine my future. I am no longer under the dominion of sin. Through the power of the Holy Spirit, I will grow in righteousness, obedience, wisdom and godly character. My life will increasingly reflect the nature of Jesus Christ. I will not merely profess Christianity; I will demonstrate the life of Christ in my daily conduct. In Jesus' name. Amen."

K. CLOSING PRAYER

* Father, thank You for the gift of salvation through Jesus Christ.
* Lord, let everyone who has been depending on religious activities without genuine conversion encounter the transforming power of the gospel.
* Holy Spirit, renew our hearts and help us overcome every form of sinful behaviour.
* Give new believers the grace to grow in knowledge, wisdom and spiritual maturity.
* Deliver the Church from hypocrisy, spiritual pride and the abuse of grace.
* Let our lives become visible testimonies of the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
* Help us remain faithful to Christ and finish our Christian journey well.

In Jesus' mighty name. Amen.

lessons.introduction:
One of the greatest struggles in human life is the struggle to understand who we really are. Many people spend their lives trying to discover their identity through education, wealth, relationships, achievements, family background, physical appearance, professional titles and social recognition.

Some people believe they are important because they have money. Others feel worthless because they come from poor families. Some define themselves by their academic qualifications, while others carry the shame of previous mistakes. There are people who have been rejected so often that they have accepted rejection as their identity.

Consider a young man who grew up in a family where nobody completed secondary school. He begins to believe that he cannot achieve anything meaningful. Even when opportunities come, he withdraws because he has already accepted the label of failure.

Consider another person who was once involved in criminal activities but has genuinely repented and surrendered his life to Christ. Although God has forgiven him, he continues to introduce himself through his past. He struggles to believe that his life can become different.

These situations reveal an important truth: what a person believes about himself can influence how he thinks, behaves, relates with others and responds to opportunities.

The gospel does not merely change a person's religious activities; it changes the foundation upon which that person's life is built.

When someone becomes a Christian, he or she receives a new identity in Christ. This does not mean that the person immediately becomes perfect, loses every weakness or forgets every painful experience. It means that the person's relationship with God, spiritual position, belonging and ultimate destiny have changed.

A believer must therefore learn to distinguish between what happened to him, what people say about him and what God declares concerning him.

Reflective question: If all your possessions, qualifications, professional titles and social recognition were taken away, would you still know who you are in Christ?

lessons.lessonContent:
RESTORATION MANDATE GOSPEL MISSION INTERNATIONAL (RMGM)
2027 SUNDAY SCHOOL MANUAL
ANNUAL THEME: BUILDING CHRIST-CENTRED LIVES FOR KINGDOM IMPACT

Date: Sunday, January 17, 2027
Central Truth: A believer's true identity is not determined by background, achievements, failures, social status or the opinions of people, but by what God has accomplished through Jesus Christ.

LESSON AIM AND OBJECTIVES
Lesson Aim: To help believers understand who they are in Christ, recognise their spiritual position and live daily in the reality of their new identity.

BIBLICAL EXPLANATION: WHAT THE TEXT MEANS

A. Ephesians 1:3–14 — The Spiritual Blessings of Our Identity in Christ

Paul's letter to the Ephesians presents one of the richest explanations of the believer's spiritual position. He begins by describing the blessings God has provided through Jesus Christ.

The repeated expression "in Christ" or "in him" is important. It teaches that Christian identity is rooted in a relationship with Jesus, not simply in religious activities.

Let us examine some of these blessings.

1. We are chosen in Christ (Ephesians 1:4).

Paul explains that God chose believers in Christ before the foundation of the world, with the purpose that they should be holy and without blame before Him in love.

This truth reveals that salvation is not an accidental arrangement. God's saving purpose is rooted in His grace and eternal wisdom.

Being chosen does not mean that a Christian should become proud or look down on others. Rather, it should produce gratitude, humility and a desire to live in a manner that honours God.

A person who understands that God's grace has brought him into His family will not boast as though he earned his position.

2. We are adopted into God's family (Ephesians 1:5).

Adoption means that God has graciously brought believers into a relationship with Himself as His children through Jesus Christ.

This is a significant change in spiritual relationship. The Christian is not merely someone who attends religious gatherings; he belongs to God's family.

In many African communities, family identity carries responsibilities, privileges and a sense of belonging. A child is expected to represent the family well. Similarly, a believer who has become part of God's family must learn to reflect the character of the Father.

3. We are accepted in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6).

Many people spend their lives seeking acceptance. They change their behaviour, appearance, opinions and values to gain the approval of others.

However, the Christian's acceptance before God is grounded in Jesus Christ.

This does not mean that God approves every action of a believer. It means that through Christ, believers are welcomed into a relationship with Him. They are no longer required to earn salvation through human performance.

A Christian who understands this truth will not make people's approval the foundation of his self-worth.

4. We have redemption and forgiveness (Ephesians 1:7).

Redemption speaks of deliverance through the price paid by Christ. Paul connects this redemption with the forgiveness of sins through the riches of God's grace.

The believer's past may contain painful experiences, mistakes and failures, but those things do not have to become the permanent definition of his life.

Forgiveness does not remove every earthly consequence of wrongdoing. A person who has stolen may still need to make restitution or face legal consequences. However, genuine repentance and faith in Christ bring forgiveness and the possibility of a transformed future.

5. We have received the Holy Spirit as the seal of God's promise (Ephesians 1:13–14).

The Holy Spirit is described as the seal and earnest of the believer's inheritance.

A seal signifies ownership and authenticity, while the earnest points to a guarantee or pledge of what is to come.

This means that the Christian life is not sustained by human strength alone. The Holy Spirit is present to empower, guide and help believers live for God.

Therefore, our identity in Christ is not merely a religious title. It is a relationship established by grace, secured in Christ and accompanied by the presence of the Holy Spirit.

B. Romans 8:14–17 — We Are Children and Heirs of God

Paul explains that those who are led by the Spirit of God are the sons of God.

1. We are children of God.

Romans 8:15 teaches that believers have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but the Spirit of adoption, whereby they cry, "Abba, Father."

The expression "Abba, Father" communicates a personal relationship with God. It shows that believers can approach Him with confidence and reverence as their Father.

This truth is especially important for people who have experienced rejection, neglect or difficult relationships with earthly parents.

A person's experience with a human father may influence how he understands fatherhood, but it must not become the final definition of God's character.

God is not limited by the failures of human parents.

2. We are led by the Spirit.

Being a child of God involves more than claiming a spiritual title. It includes learning to follow the leadership of the Holy Spirit.

A believer cannot continually reject God's instruction while confidently claiming to be walking in the Spirit.

The Spirit leads us towards obedience, holiness, truth, love and Christlike character.

3. We are heirs of God and joint-heirs with Christ.

Romans 8:17 teaches that believers are heirs of God and joint-heirs with Christ, while also acknowledging that suffering with Christ precedes sharing in His glory.

This is a powerful reminder that Christian identity does not guarantee a life without difficulty.

A believer may experience persecution, disappointment, financial pressure or personal struggles. Such experiences do not automatically mean that God has abandoned him.

Our inheritance in Christ gives us hope beyond present circumstances.

C. 1 Peter 2:9–10 — Our Identity and Our Responsibility

Peter describes believers using four powerful expressions.

1. A chosen generation

Believers belong to a people called by God's grace. Their identity is not defined by ethnic superiority, social class or family background.

2. A royal priesthood

This expression combines the ideas of royalty and priesthood. Believers belong to God's kingdom and are called to serve Him.

The priesthood of all believers means that every Christian has access to God through Jesus Christ and a responsibility to represent Him in the world.

It does not mean that all believers hold the same ministry office or authority.

3. A holy nation

Holiness means being set apart for God. Christians are called to live differently from the sinful values and practices of the world.

Holiness is not merely about outward appearance, dressing or religious language. It must affect honesty, sexuality, business conduct, family relationships, speech, money management and treatment of others.

4. A peculiar people

The word describes a people belonging to God as His own possession.

Our identity should therefore be visible in our conduct.

Peter concludes by explaining the purpose: believers are called to show forth the praises or excellencies of the One who called them out of darkness into His marvellous light.

In other words, our identity is not given merely for personal comfort; it carries a responsibility to make God's goodness known.

D. Colossians 3:1–4 — Living from Our New Position

Paul teaches that if believers are risen with Christ, they should seek those things which are above.

This passage does not teach that Christians should abandon their earthly responsibilities. Rather, it teaches that their priorities, values and decisions must be shaped by their relationship with Christ.

A Christian should not become careless about education, work, family, business or civic responsibilities under the excuse of being spiritually minded.

Instead, the believer should approach these responsibilities with a renewed understanding of God's priorities.

Our life is hid with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3).

This means that the believer's deepest security and ultimate identity are found in Christ.

People may misunderstand you. Circumstances may change. Your financial condition may rise or fall. However, your position in Christ remains the foundation of your spiritual confidence.

Paul also points towards the future manifestation of believers with Christ in glory. Christian identity therefore has a present reality and a future hope.

THEOLOGICAL CLARIFICATION: AVOIDING EXTREMES

Understanding identity in Christ requires biblical balance. Some teachings can distort this truth when important distinctions are ignored.

1. Identity in Christ is not a licence for pride.

Being chosen, adopted and accepted by God should produce humility, not superiority.

No believer has grounds to despise another person. Salvation is a gift of grace.

2. Identity in Christ does not mean that Christians never struggle.

A believer may still battle with temptation, emotional pain, weaknesses and difficult circumstances.

The difference is that these struggles no longer have to define his spiritual position or control his future. He must continue to grow in Christ.

3. Forgiveness does not automatically cancel earthly consequences.

A person who has repented of fraud must still take responsibility for restitution where possible. A person who has damaged relationships should seek reconciliation appropriately.

Grace provides forgiveness and transformation, not an excuse to avoid responsibility.

4. Being a child of God does not mean receiving everything we desire.

God's fatherhood must not be reduced to a promise of unlimited wealth, comfort or freedom from suffering.

Romans 8:17 reminds us that suffering can form part of the Christian journey.

5. Spiritual identity does not eliminate the need for personal development.

A Christian still needs education, discipline, emotional maturity, professional competence, financial responsibility and healthy relationships.

Knowing who you are in Christ should motivate you to develop your God-given abilities, not neglect them.

DOCTRINAL ALIGNMENT

This lesson agrees with the following biblical doctrines:

- Creation and human dignity: Every human being is created in God's image and possesses dignity (Genesis 1:26–27).
- Salvation by grace: Believers are saved through faith, not by their own works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
- Union with Christ: The believer's new spiritual position is established through relationship with Jesus Christ (Ephesians 1:3–7).
- Adoption: Those who belong to Christ are brought into God's family (Romans 8:14–17).
- Sanctification: Believers are called to grow in holiness and Christlike character (1 Thessalonians 4:3).
- Christian hope: The believer's future is secured in Christ, with the promise of sharing in His glory (Colossians 3:4).

KEY TRUTHS / LESSON HIGHLIGHTS

- Your identity is determined by your relationship with Christ, not your circumstances.
- You are not required to earn God's acceptance through human performance.
- In Christ, you are forgiven, adopted and brought into God's family.
- Your past may explain some of your experiences, but it does not have to determine your future.
- Being a child of God carries responsibilities as well as privileges.
- Your identity should influence your behaviour, relationships and decisions.
- Christian maturity involves learning to live consistently with what God has declared about you.

LIFE APPLICATION

How should this lesson influence our daily lives?

A. In the family

A parent who understands his or her identity in Christ should not use insults, rejection or violence to control children. Instead, the parent should demonstrate God's love through discipline, patience and responsible leadership.

Children should also learn that their value does not depend on comparing themselves with siblings or other children.

B. In education and career

A student's identity should not be determined by examination results. Failure in one examination does not make someone a failure in life.

A Christian should respond to poor performance by learning, improving and seeking help rather than surrendering to shame.

C. In business and professional life

A believer should not compromise integrity to gain financial advantage. Being a child of God must influence how contracts are handled, employees are treated, customers are served and money is managed.

D. In relationships

People who understand their identity in Christ should not remain in destructive relationships merely because they fear rejection.

They should learn healthy boundaries, mutual respect, forgiveness and responsible communication. Where there is abuse or danger, seeking appropriate protection and assistance is necessary.

E. In the church

No Christian should feel inferior because of financial status, educational qualification, tribe, gender or social position.

Likewise, church leaders must not use spiritual titles to intimidate or exploit members.

Every believer has dignity and responsibility within the body of Christ.

F. In personal development

A Christian should not use grace as an excuse for laziness. Rather, the knowledge that God has given him purpose should inspire excellence, discipline, learning and responsible living.

CASE STUDY / REAL-LIFE SCENARIO

Case Study: The Man Who Could Not Move Beyond His Past

Emmanuel grew up in a troubled environment. During his teenage years, he became involved in stealing, fighting and other destructive activities. In his early twenties, he was arrested and spent time in prison.

While there, he encountered Christian ministers, began studying the Bible and eventually surrendered his life to Christ. After his release, he joined a local church and became actively involved in Christian fellowship.

However, Emmanuel continued to struggle with his past. Whenever someone praised his progress, he dismissed it. He believed that he could never become a responsible person because of what he had done.

Some church members also continued to remind him of his past. They were unwilling to trust him with responsibilities, even after observing genuine changes in his conduct.

As a result, Emmanuel became discouraged and began withdrawing from fellowship.

Questions for Discussion:

- What factors are influencing Emmanuel's understanding of himself?
- How should Ephesians 1:7 and 2 Corinthians 5:17 influence his understanding of his new life?

- What practical steps can Emmanuel take to rebuild trust and develop his abilities?
- How should the church balance wisdom, accountability, restoration and acceptance?
- What can we learn from Emmanuel's experience about the way we treat people with difficult pasts?

Teaching Insight:

The church must not become a place where people are permanently imprisoned by their past. Genuine transformation should be recognised and encouraged, while wisdom, accountability and demonstrated character remain important.

A person's past should neither be ignored nor allowed to become the permanent definition of his future.

PERSONAL REFLECTION AND ACTION POINT

Take a few minutes to examine your understanding of yourself.

- Do I define myself more by what people say about me than by what God says in His Word?
- Am I still carrying guilt over sins I have genuinely confessed and forsaken?
- Do I feel inferior because of my family background, financial condition or educational level?
- Does my behaviour reflect the identity I claim to have in Christ?
- Do I treat other believers with the dignity and respect that God's family deserves?

Personal declaration:

I belong to Jesus Christ. My identity is established by God's grace. I am forgiven through Christ, adopted into God's family and called to live a holy and purposeful life. My past will not become the master of my future. I will grow in character, walk in obedience and represent Christ faithfully wherever I find myself. Amen.

INVITATION TO SALVATION

It is important to understand that identity in Christ begins with a genuine relationship with Jesus.

Church attendance, Christian family background, religious titles and participation in ministry activities cannot replace personal repentance and faith in Christ.

If you have never surrendered your life to Jesus, today is an opportunity to begin.

Romans 10:9 teaches that salvation involves believing in the heart that God raised Jesus from the dead and confessing Him as Lord.

Suggested prayer of commitment:

Lord Jesus, I acknowledge that I am a sinner and that I need Your salvation. I believe that You died for my sins and rose again. Today, I repent of my sins and surrender my life to You. Forgive me, make me new and receive me into Your family. Help me to know You, follow Your Word and live according to Your purpose. Fill me with Your Holy Spirit and teach me to walk in my new identity. In Jesus' name, Amen.

This prayer is not a formula that automatically saves. Salvation is received through genuine repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.

ACTION POINT FOR THE WEEK

WEEKLY ASSIGNMENT

During this week, every participant should undertake the following exercises:

- Study: Read Ephesians 1:3–14 every day and identify at least one spiritual blessing mentioned in the passage.
- Write: List five negative labels or beliefs you have accepted about yourself that contradict biblical truth. Beside each one, write a relevant biblical truth.
- Practise: Make one deliberate decision this week that reflects your identity in Christ, even when it is unpopular.
- Restore: Identify one person you may have judged or treated unfairly because of their background or past. Take an appropriate step towards treating that person with dignity.
- Develop: Identify one area of your life—spiritual, emotional, educational, professional, financial or relational—that needs growth. Write down one practical step you will take.

CLOSING PRAYER

Heavenly Father, thank You for bringing us into Your family through Jesus Christ. Open our understanding to know who we are in You. Deliver us from the bondage of shame, rejection, inferiority and false identities. Help us to stop measuring our worth by material possessions, social recognition and the opinions of people.

Teach us to walk in holiness, humility, confidence and love. May our families, workplaces, businesses, churches and communities experience the positive influence of our new identity in Christ. Help us to represent You faithfully and grow into mature disciples.

In Jesus' mighty name. Amen.

CONCLUSION

Understanding our identity in Christ is foundational to Christian maturity. A believer who does not understand who he is may continually seek validation from people, surrender to destructive pressures or allow past experiences to control his decisions.

However, the person who understands his position in Christ learns to live from a foundation of acceptance, forgiveness, belonging and hope.

We must remember that our identity is both a privilege and a responsibility. We are called out of darkness not merely to enjoy the benefits of salvation but to demonstrate the character and excellencies of the One who saved us.

The goal is not simply to know that we belong to Christ, but to live every day in a manner that makes our belonging evident.

Teacher's Final Emphasis: You must know who you are in Christ before you can consistently live the life Christ expects from you. Identity must produce character, and character must produce kingdom impact.

lessons.theme: The authority of Scripture in everyday Christian living
lessons.memoryVerse: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:" — 2 Timothy 3:16 (KJV)
lessons.introduction:
We live in a world filled with information. Every day, people receive advice from social media, television, religious leaders, friends, family members, motivational speakers, political commentators and various online platforms.

Some of this information is useful, some is misleading, and some is completely destructive.

A person may receive one instruction from a parent, another from a friend, a different opinion from a social media influencer and yet another from a religious teacher. When these instructions conflict, the question becomes: What standard should guide our decisions?

Consider a young Christian who works in an organisation where employees are expected to falsify financial records. His colleagues explain that everyone does it and that refusing to participate may cost him his job. He begins to wonder whether honesty is still practical in the present economic environment.

Consider a married woman who receives advice from friends that revenge is the best response to an unfaithful spouse. She is encouraged to humiliate her husband publicly rather than seek a responsible path towards addressing the situation.

Consider a young person who spends several hours daily watching online content that gradually influences his understanding of relationships, sexuality, money, success and morality. Although he attends church every Sunday, his daily decisions are increasingly shaped by what he consumes online.

These examples reveal a serious challenge: many Christians attend church, own Bibles and listen to sermons, but their everyday decisions are not necessarily governed by Scripture.

The Bible was not given merely to decorate our homes, provide quotations for social media or serve as a religious textbook. It is God's revealed Word, given to guide His people into truth and godly living.

A Christian who does not allow Scripture to shape his thinking will eventually be shaped by another authority.

The purpose of this lesson is to establish that God's Word must become the foundation of our beliefs, choices, values and conduct.

Reflective question: If your daily decisions were examined, would people discover that the Bible is truly the authority governing your life?
