lessons.lessonContent:
RESTORATION MANDATE GOSPEL MISSION INTERNATIONAL (RMGM)
2027 SUNDAY SCHOOL MANUAL
ANNUAL THEME: BUILDING CHRIST-CENTRED LIVES FOR KINGDOM IMPACT

Date: Sunday, January 24, 2027
Central Truth: The Word of God is the supreme authority for Christian faith and conduct. A mature believer does not merely read the Bible but allows its truth to shape decisions, attitudes, relationships and everyday behaviour.

LESSON AIM AND OBJECTIVES
Lesson Aim: To establish the authority, reliability and practical relevance of Scripture in the life of every Christian, and to encourage believers to become consistent hearers and doers of God's Word.

BIBLICAL EXPLANATION: WHAT THE TEXT MEANS

A. Psalm 119:9–16 — The Word of God as a Guide for Pure Living

Psalm 119 is a celebration of the Word of God. It presents Scripture as a source of direction, wisdom, spiritual nourishment and moral guidance.

In verses 9–16, the psalmist focuses on how a young person can maintain a pure life in a world filled with competing influences.

1. The Word of God provides direction for a pure life (verse 9).

The psalmist asks:

"Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word."

This question is relevant to every generation. Young people face pressures relating to sexuality, peer influence, dishonesty, substance abuse, violence and the pursuit of material success.

However, the principle is not limited to young people. Every believer needs God's Word to maintain a life that pleases Him.

The expression "taking heed" means paying careful attention and responding appropriately.

It is not enough to know what the Bible says. We must allow its instructions to influence our conduct.

For example, a Christian who knows that the Bible condemns dishonesty but continues to manipulate business transactions has information without obedience.

2. We must seek God with the whole heart (verse 10).

The psalmist declares that he has sought God with his whole heart.

This teaches that biblical obedience grows out of a genuine relationship with God.

Some people study Scripture only to win arguments, criticise others or acquire religious knowledge. But the purpose of knowing God's Word is to know Him better and live according to His will.

A person may have extensive biblical knowledge without possessing a surrendered heart.

3. God's Word must be stored in our hearts (verse 11).

"Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee."

To hide God's Word in the heart means to treasure, remember and internalise it.

When a person memorises and meditates on Scripture, biblical truth becomes available to guide decisions even when a Bible is not physically nearby.

A young person who has internalised biblical teachings on purity may find strength to resist sexual pressure. A business owner who has internalised biblical principles of honesty may refuse to falsify accounts even when no one is watching.

However, memorising Scripture must not become a substitute for obeying it. The Word must move from memory into conduct.

4. We must delight in God's commandments (verses 12–16).

The psalmist describes God's statutes as something in which he delights.

This is an important attitude. Christian obedience should not be based solely on fear of punishment or pressure from religious leaders.

As believers grow spiritually, they learn to value God's instructions because they recognise His wisdom and goodness.

A Christian who delights in God's Word will seek opportunities to understand and practise it.

B. 2 Timothy 3:14–17 — The Inspiration and Purpose of Scripture

Paul writes to Timothy, a younger minister whom he has trained in the faith. He reminds him of the Scriptures he has known from childhood.

This passage provides a foundational explanation of why the Bible is authoritative.

1. Scripture is inspired by God (verse 16).

The King James Version says:

"All scripture is given by inspiration of God..."

The expression translated "inspiration of God" communicates that Scripture is God-breathed.

The Bible did not originate merely from human imagination, philosophical speculation or cultural tradition. God worked through human authors, using their personalities, backgrounds and historical circumstances to communicate His message.

This does not mean that every human interpretation of the Bible is automatically correct. It means that the Scriptures themselves are divinely inspired and therefore deserve our trust and reverence.

2. Scripture is profitable for doctrine.

Doctrine means teaching or instruction concerning what Christians should believe.

The Bible teaches us about:

- God and His character.
- Creation and humanity.
- Sin and its consequences.
- Salvation through Jesus Christ.
- The Holy Spirit and Christian living.
- The church and its mission.
- The return of Christ and eternal life.

Without sound biblical teaching, Christians can easily accept false doctrines and misleading spiritual claims.

3. Scripture is profitable for reproof.

Reproof means exposing error or showing where something is wrong.

The Word of God acts like a mirror that reveals attitudes, actions and beliefs that are inconsistent with God's will.

For example, a person may believe he is generous but discover through Scripture that he neglects the needs of vulnerable family members while spending extravagantly on himself.

Another may consider himself spiritually mature but discover that his speech is filled with insults, gossip and bitterness.

The Word exposes these inconsistencies so that genuine change can begin.

4. Scripture is profitable for correction.

Correction goes beyond identifying what is wrong. It provides direction towards what is right.

A person who has been dishonest can learn to practise integrity. Someone who has been harsh can learn gentleness. A believer who has neglected prayer can begin rebuilding a consistent devotional life.

God's Word does not merely condemn wrongdoing; it provides a path towards restoration and obedience.

5. Scripture is profitable for instruction in righteousness.

This means that God's Word trains believers to live in a manner that pleases Him.

Christian maturity does not happen automatically. It requires learning, discipline, correction and consistent practice.

6. Scripture equips the believer for every good work (verse 17).

Paul explains that the purpose of Scripture is that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works.

The word "perfect" here carries the idea of being complete or equipped.

The Bible prepares believers to serve God effectively. It equips parents to guide children, leaders to exercise responsibility, workers to demonstrate integrity, young people to make wise choices and Christians to serve their communities.

The Word is therefore relevant to the whole of life, not only to activities within the church building.

C. Hebrews 4:12 — The Living and Powerful Word of God

Hebrews describes the Word of God as quick and powerful, sharper than any two-edged sword.

The expression "quick" in the King James Version means living.

1. God's Word is living.

Unlike ordinary human opinions that may become outdated, God's Word continues to speak with divine authority across generations.

The Bible addresses the fundamental realities of human existence: sin, righteousness, love, justice, forgiveness, suffering, hope, relationships and accountability.

Its message remains relevant because human nature and our need for God have not changed.

2. God's Word is powerful.

The Word is not merely information. It is a means through which God confronts, teaches, convicts and transforms people.

When someone reads about forgiveness, the Word can expose bitterness. When someone studies biblical teachings on stewardship, it can challenge financial irresponsibility.

The Word can disturb a person's comfort with wrongdoing and encourage a new direction.

3. God's Word penetrates the inner person.

Hebrews 4:12 speaks of the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, joints and marrow, and the discernment of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

The point is that God's Word reaches deeply into the inner life of a person.

People may deceive others with outward religious behaviour, but Scripture exposes the motives behind their actions.

A person may give money publicly to gain recognition, preach to gain influence or serve in church to receive praise. God's Word challenges such motives and calls for sincerity.

D. James 1:22–25 — The Word Must Be Practised

James provides one of the clearest warnings against hearing Scripture without obedience.

1. Hearing without doing is self-deception (verse 22).

James writes:

"But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves."

A person can attend church every Sunday, listen to sermons, take notes and participate in Bible studies without allowing the Word to change his behaviour.

The danger is that religious activity may create the impression of spiritual maturity even when practical obedience is absent.

For example, a man may regularly attend marriage seminars but continue to abuse his wife. A Christian business owner may quote Bible verses while exploiting employees. A church worker may preach forgiveness but refuse to reconcile with a family member.

The problem is not a lack of hearing. It is a failure to practise what has been heard.

2. God's Word is like a mirror (verses 23–24).

James compares a hearer who does not obey the Word to someone who looks at his natural face in a mirror and immediately forgets what he looks like.

A mirror reveals what needs attention. But looking into a mirror without responding to what it reveals makes the exercise unproductive.

Similarly, Scripture may reveal anger, pride, dishonesty, sexual immorality, greed or unforgiveness. The correct response is repentance and practical change.

3. The doer of the Word experiences blessing (verse 25).

James describes the person who continues in the perfect law of liberty and becomes a doer of the work as blessed in his deed.

Obedience is not a means of purchasing salvation. Rather, it is evidence of a life that takes God's Word seriously.

A person who practises biblical wisdom is better positioned to develop healthy relationships, maintain integrity, make responsible decisions and experience the benefits of godly living.

THEOLOGICAL CLARIFICATION: AVOIDING EXTREMES

To understand biblical authority properly, believers must avoid several errors.

1. The Bible must not be treated as a collection of isolated quotations.

A verse should be understood within its chapter, book, historical setting and overall biblical message.

Taking Scripture out of context can produce false teachings and harmful applications.

2. Personal revelation must not replace Scripture.

God may guide believers through prayer, the Holy Spirit, godly counsel and circumstances. However, no claimed revelation should be used to contradict the clear teaching of Scripture.

A person cannot justify dishonesty, sexual immorality, exploitation or abuse by claiming that God privately instructed him to do so.

3. The Bible must not be reduced to a book of prosperity promises.

Scripture teaches about provision and stewardship, but it also addresses suffering, sacrifice, contentment, generosity and faithfulness.

A believer must study the whole counsel of God rather than select only passages that promise material benefits.

4. Biblical authority does not mean blind acceptance of every religious interpretation.

Pastors, teachers and church leaders must be evaluated in the light of Scripture.

The Berean believers were commended because they examined the Scriptures to determine whether the things they heard were true (Acts 17:10–11).

Respect for spiritual leadership does not require abandoning biblical discernment.

5. Knowledge without obedience is not Christian maturity.

A person may know many Bible passages and still be dishonest, proud, abusive or irresponsible.

The true test of biblical learning is not merely how much Scripture we can quote, but how faithfully we live according to it.

6. Scripture must be interpreted responsibly in contemporary situations.

The Bible may not mention modern inventions such as smartphones, social media platforms or artificial intelligence by name. However, its principles concerning truthfulness, purity, stewardship, love, wisdom and responsibility guide how believers use these technologies.

DOCTRINAL ALIGNMENT

This lesson agrees with the following biblical doctrines:

- Divine inspiration: Scripture is given by inspiration of God (2 Timothy 3:16).
- Biblical authority: God's Word provides the standard for Christian belief and conduct (Psalm 119:105).
- Divine revelation: God has made Himself known through His revealed Word and supremely through Jesus Christ (Hebrews 1:1–2).
- Spiritual transformation: Believers are transformed through the renewal of their minds (Romans 12:2).
- Sanctification: God's truth works in the life of believers as they grow in holiness (John 17:17).
- Christian obedience: Genuine faith produces practical obedience to God's Word (James 1:22–25).

KEY TRUTHS / LESSON HIGHLIGHTS

- The Bible is inspired by God and authoritative for Christian faith and conduct.
- Scripture provides direction for moral and spiritual living.
- God's Word teaches, corrects, exposes error and trains believers in righteousness.
- Biblical knowledge must move beyond the mind into practical behaviour.
- Every Christian must develop the discipline of personal Bible study.
- Religious leaders and popular opinions must be tested against Scripture.
- God's Word is relevant to family life, education, business, leadership, relationships and national development.
- A mature Christian is not merely a hearer of the Word but a consistent doer.

LIFE APPLICATION

How should the authority of Scripture influence our everyday lives?

A. In the home and family

Parents should allow biblical principles to guide the upbringing of their children.

Ephesians 6:4 warns fathers against provoking their children to wrath and instructs them to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.

This means Christian parenting should not be based on intimidation, humiliation or uncontrolled anger.

Children should also learn to honour their parents and develop responsible behaviour.

B. In marriage and relationships

Biblical principles should guide love, communication, forgiveness, faithfulness and respect.

A husband should not use Scripture to justify domination or violence. A wife should not use manipulation or revenge as a substitute for healthy communication.

Both must learn to practise the biblical principles of love and mutual responsibility.

C. In business and professional life

The Bible teaches honesty, diligence, fairness and responsible stewardship.

A Christian should not falsify records, cheat customers, steal public funds, exploit workers or manipulate contracts.

Proverbs 11:1 condemns a false balance and teaches that dishonest business practices are an abomination to the Lord.

D. In education

Students should allow Scripture to guide their attitude towards learning, honesty and discipline.

Examination malpractice, plagiarism, bullying and deliberate laziness are inconsistent with Christian character.

E. In social media and digital life

Philippians 4:8 provides principles for evaluating what we allow to occupy our minds.

Christians should be careful about the content they watch, share, comment on and promote.

A believer should not spread false information, participate in online bullying or use digital platforms to destroy people's reputations.

F. In church life

Church members should evaluate teachings through Scripture rather than accepting every claim because it comes from a popular preacher.

Church leaders must also submit their teaching and conduct to biblical accountability.

G. In national and community life

Scripture teaches justice, compassion, honesty and responsibility.

Christians should oppose corruption, reject tribal discrimination, respect human dignity and contribute to the development of their communities.

The authority of Scripture should be visible not only in church services but also in the way Christians participate in society.

CASE STUDY / REAL-LIFE SCENARIO

Case Study: The Christian Businessman and the False Financial Records

Mr. Ade is a successful businessman and a committed member of his local church. He attends Sunday services regularly, participates in Bible studies and often shares Scripture on social media.

Recently, he secured a contract that could significantly improve his business. However, the organisation offering the contract requested that he inflate the financial figures and provide false documentation to qualify for a larger payment.

His accountant warned him that the arrangement was dishonest. But some business associates advised him not to miss the opportunity, arguing that business is about survival and that everyone manipulates figures.

Mr. Ade began to justify the decision by saying that the additional money would help him support his church and finance missionary work.

He eventually asked a church leader for advice.

Questions for Discussion:

- What is the major spiritual problem confronting Mr. Ade?
- Can a good intention justify a dishonest business practice?
- How should 2 Timothy 3:16 and Proverbs 11:1 influence his decision?
- What could be the long-term consequences of falsifying financial records?
- How can Christians remain faithful to Scripture in an environment where dishonesty appears normal?
- What should Mr. Ade do if refusing the arrangement means losing the contract?

Teaching Insight:

Good intentions cannot make wrongdoing acceptable before God. A person cannot finance God's work through dishonest practices and claim that the end justifies the means.

Christian integrity must be maintained even when obedience appears financially costly.

The Word of God must govern our decisions when obedience is easy and when it is difficult.

PERSONAL REFLECTION AND ACTION POINT

Take time to examine your relationship with Scripture.

- Do I read the Bible consistently or only when I attend church?
- Do I study Scripture to understand God's will or merely to find quotations?
- Are there areas of my life where I deliberately disobey what I already know?
- Do I allow popular opinions to influence me more than biblical truth?
- Can my family and colleagues recognise biblical values in my conduct?
- What specific area of my life needs correction through God's Word?

Personal declaration:

The Word of God is my authority and guide. I will not allow popular opinions, social pressure or personal convenience to replace biblical truth. I will study the Scriptures, meditate on their message and obey their instructions. My decisions, relationships, work and service will reflect the wisdom of God's Word. By His grace, I will become not only a hearer but a faithful doer of the Word. Amen.

ACTION POINT FOR THE WEEK

WEEKLY ASSIGNMENT

Every participant should complete the following exercises during the week:

- Daily Bible reading: Read Psalm 119:9–16 every day and write down one lesson from the passage.
- Personal study: Study 2 Timothy 3:14–17 and identify the four major benefits of Scripture mentioned in verse 16.
- Application: Identify one area of your life where your conduct does not fully agree with biblical teaching. Write down the correction you need to make.
- Memorisation: Memorise 2 Timothy 3:16 and explain its meaning in your own words to another person.
- Family or group practice: Organise a short Bible discussion with your family, friends or fellowship group. Discuss one biblical principle and agree on how to practise it during the week.

CLOSING PRAYER

Heavenly Father, we thank You for giving us Your Word as a guide for our lives. Give us a deeper hunger for the Scriptures and the wisdom to understand them correctly.

Deliver us from ignorance, deception and the influence of teachings that contradict Your truth. Help us to recognise areas of our lives that require correction and give us the courage to obey You even when obedience is difficult.

Let Your Word guide our homes, marriages, businesses, education, leadership and relationships. May we become Christians whose lives demonstrate the truth we profess.

Raise in us a generation of believers who are not merely hearers of the Word but faithful doers, bringing positive transformation to our churches, communities and nation.

In Jesus' mighty name. Amen.

CONCLUSION

The authority of Scripture is one of the foundations of Christian maturity. A believer who neglects God's Word becomes vulnerable to deception, worldly pressure and spiritual instability.

The Bible provides the standard by which our beliefs, values, decisions and conduct must be examined.

However, the goal of studying Scripture is not merely to accumulate biblical information. It is to know God, become more like Christ and faithfully practise His instructions.

We must therefore develop a lifestyle of reading, studying, meditating on and obeying God's Word.

A Christian whose life is governed by Scripture will be better equipped to face challenges, make responsible decisions, build healthy relationships and contribute meaningfully to society.

Teacher's Final Emphasis: The Bible must not merely be the book we carry to church; it must become the authority that guides the lives we live outside the church.

LIFE APPLICATION

A. In the home and family
Parents should allow biblical principles to guide the upbringing of their children. Ephesians 6:4 warns fathers against provoking their children to wrath and instructs them to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. This means Christian parenting should not be based on intimidation, humiliation or uncontrolled anger. Children should also learn to honour their parents and develop responsible behaviour.

B. In marriage and relationships
Biblical principles should guide love, communication, forgiveness, faithfulness and respect. A husband should not use Scripture to justify domination or violence. A wife should not use manipulation or revenge as a substitute for healthy communication. Both must learn to practise the biblical principles of love and mutual responsibility.

C. In business and professional life
The Bible teaches honesty, diligence, fairness and responsible stewardship. A Christian should not falsify records, cheat customers, steal public funds, exploit workers or manipulate contracts. Proverbs 11:1 condemns a false balance and teaches that dishonest business practices are an abomination to the Lord.

D. In education
Students should allow Scripture to guide their attitude towards learning, honesty and discipline. Examination malpractice, plagiarism, bullying and deliberate laziness are inconsistent with Christian character.

E. In social media and digital life
Philippians 4:8 provides principles for evaluating what we allow to occupy our minds. Christians should be careful about the content they watch, share, comment on and promote. A believer should not spread false information, participate in online bullying or use digital platforms to destroy people's reputations.

F. In church life
Church members should evaluate teachings through Scripture rather than accepting every claim because it comes from a popular preacher. Church leaders must also submit their teaching and conduct to biblical accountability.

G. In national and community life
Scripture teaches justice, compassion, honesty and responsibility. Christians should oppose corruption, reject tribal discrimination, respect human dignity and contribute to the development of their communities. The authority of Scripture should be visible not only in church services but also in the way Christians participate in society.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Salvation, Grace and the Responsibility of Christian Living
lessons.theme: Salvation, grace and the responsibility of Christian living
lessons.memoryVerse:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:

Not of works, lest any man should boast." — Ephesians 2:8–9 (KJV)
lessons.introduction:
One of the greatest misunderstandings in Christianity is the relationship between God's grace and human responsibility.

Some people believe that because salvation is by grace, Christians do not need to make serious efforts to live holy lives. They argue that God understands their weaknesses and will forgive them regardless of how they behave.

Others believe that they must work hard enough, give enough offerings, attend enough church programmes, fast sufficiently or perform enough religious activities to earn God's acceptance.

Both positions misunderstand the biblical message.

Consider a man who was rescued from a burning building. After receiving help, he does not claim that he saved himself. He recognises that someone intervened to preserve his life. However, his rescue should change the way he lives. He should not deliberately return to the same danger without reason.

Similarly, salvation is God's intervention in the life of humanity. We were unable to rescue ourselves from the power and consequences of sin. Jesus Christ came, died for our sins and rose again to provide the way of reconciliation with God.

We did not purchase this salvation. We did not earn it through good behaviour. It is a gift of God's grace.

However, the grace that saves us also calls us into a new way of living.

A person who claims to have received God's grace but deliberately continues to embrace dishonesty, sexual immorality, exploitation, hatred and rebellion without repentance has misunderstood the purpose of salvation.

Christianity is not simply receiving forgiveness while continuing to live as before. It is receiving a new life in Christ and learning to walk in the reality of that life.

Reflective question: If salvation is a free gift, why does God still expect Christians to live responsibly and obey His Word?

lessons.lessonContent:
RESTORATION MANDATE GOSPEL MISSION INTERNATIONAL (RMGM)
2027 SUNDAY SCHOOL MANUAL
ANNUAL THEME: BUILDING CHRIST-CENTRED LIVES FOR KINGDOM IMPACT

Date: Sunday, January 31, 2027
Central Truth: Salvation is God's gracious gift received through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward for human effort. However, genuine salvation produces a transformed life characterised by obedience, holiness, good works and responsibility.

LESSON AIM AND OBJECTIVES
Lesson Aim: To help believers understand the biblical meaning of salvation and grace, appreciate what Christ has accomplished for them, and recognise their responsibility to live in a manner that reflects the salvation they have received.

BIBLICAL EXPLANATION: WHAT THE TEXT MEANS

A. Ephesians 2:1–10 — Salvation Is a Gift of God's Grace

Paul's letter to the Ephesians provides one of the clearest explanations of salvation.

He begins by describing humanity's condition before coming to Christ and then explains what God has done through His mercy.

1. Our condition before salvation: spiritually dead in sin (verses 1–3).

Paul describes people as being dead in trespasses and sins.

This does not mean that they were physically dead. It means that sin had separated them from the life and fellowship of God.

He identifies three influences that characterised their former way of life:

- The course or pattern of the world.
- The influence of the prince of the power of the air.
- The desires of the flesh and the mind.

This passage reveals that sin is more than individual mistakes. It is a condition that affects human nature, relationships, desires and choices.

For example, corruption may become so normalised in a society that people no longer consider it wrong. A young person may participate in cultism because friends have presented it as a means of protection or influence. A business owner may practise fraud because competitors are doing the same thing.

These examples show how individuals can become influenced by destructive patterns around them.

Paul's description teaches that humanity needs more than moral advice. We need spiritual rescue.

2. God's intervention: rich in mercy and great in love (verses 4–5).

The passage changes direction with the words, "But God."

Humanity was helpless in sin, but God intervened because of His mercy and love.

God did not wait for humanity to become perfect before making salvation available. He acted through Jesus Christ.

This is the foundation of grace: God provides what sinful humanity cannot achieve by its own strength.

3. Salvation is by grace through faith (verses 8–9).

Paul explains that salvation is God's gift, not the product of human works.

Grace means God's undeserved favour and saving kindness.

Faith is the response of trusting in Jesus Christ and relying on what He has accomplished.

A person cannot purchase salvation through money, religious titles, charitable activities or personal achievements.

A wealthy individual and a poor individual must both come to God through the same way: faith in Jesus Christ.

This truth destroys spiritual pride. Nobody can boast as though salvation is a personal achievement.

4. We are created in Christ for good works (verse 10).

This verse is essential to understanding the relationship between grace and responsibility.

Paul explains that believers are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works.

Notice the order:

- We are not saved by good works.
- We are saved by grace through faith.
- We are saved for a life of good works.

Good works are not the foundation of salvation; they are the fruit and evidence of genuine salvation.

A person who claims to have received Christ should increasingly demonstrate the character of Christ.

For example, a person who previously cheated customers should begin practising honesty. Someone who was violent should learn self-control. A person who neglected family responsibilities should begin taking responsibility for the people entrusted to him.

These changes do not purchase salvation. They demonstrate the transforming influence of God's grace.

B. Romans 5:1–11 — The Benefits of Salvation Through Jesus Christ

Paul explains the blessings that believers receive through justification by faith.

1. We have peace with God (verse 1).

Justification means that God declares the believer righteous on the basis of Christ's saving work.

Through faith in Jesus Christ, the hostility caused by sin is dealt with, and the believer is reconciled to God.

This peace is deeper than the absence of personal problems. It is the restored relationship between God and the believer.

A Christian may still experience family challenges, financial difficulties or opposition, but these circumstances do not automatically mean that the person has lost peace with God.

2. We have access to God's grace (verse 2).

Paul teaches that through Christ, believers have access by faith into the grace in which they stand.

The Christian life is sustained by God's grace.

We need grace not only at the moment of conversion but throughout our journey of faith.

We need grace to overcome temptation, forgive others, endure difficulties, develop godly character and fulfil our responsibilities.

3. We have hope even in suffering (verses 3–5).

Romans 5 teaches that believers can glory in tribulations because suffering can produce perseverance, proven character and hope.

This does not mean that Christians should enjoy pain or pretend that suffering is easy.

It means that hardship does not have to become wasted experience. As believers depend on God, difficult seasons can develop endurance and mature character.

Consider a Christian who loses a business because of an economic downturn. Rather than turning to fraud or abandoning faith, the person learns to rebuild responsibly, improve business skills and trust God through the process.

The situation may remain difficult, but the believer's response can become a testimony of grace.

4. God's love is demonstrated through Christ's death (verses 6–8).

Paul reminds believers that Christ died for the ungodly while they were still sinners.

God's love was not a reward for human goodness. It was demonstrated when humanity was unable to rescue itself.

This should produce deep gratitude and humility.

5. We are reconciled to God through Christ (verses 9–11).

Reconciliation means the restoration of a broken relationship.

Sin separated humanity from God, but through the death of Jesus Christ, believers are brought into a restored relationship with Him.

This reconciliation should influence how we relate with others.

A person who has received mercy from God should learn to show mercy. Someone who has been forgiven should be willing to pursue forgiveness and reconciliation where appropriate.

C. Titus 2:11–14 — Grace Teaches Us How to Live

This passage is particularly important because it explains that grace does more than save.

1. God's grace has appeared to bring salvation (verse 11).

Paul describes God's saving grace as having appeared to all people.

The offer of salvation is not restricted by nationality, social class, educational level or economic status.

The gospel is for humanity.

2. Grace teaches us to reject ungodliness (verse 12).

Paul explains that grace teaches believers to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts.

This means grace is not permission to continue in sin.

The grace of God trains us to say no to destructive desires and yes to godly living.

For example:

- Grace teaches a dishonest person to embrace truth.
- Grace teaches an immoral person to pursue sexual purity.
- Grace teaches a proud person to develop humility.
- Grace teaches a greedy person to practise generosity.
- Grace teaches an angry person to develop self-control.

The Christian does not overcome these behaviours merely through willpower. He depends on the Holy Spirit and the instruction of God's Word.

3. We are called to live soberly, righteously and godly (verse 12).

These three expressions cover important dimensions of Christian life.

- Soberly: Self-control, discipline and responsible personal conduct.
- Righteously: Right conduct towards other people.
- Godly: A life that honours God.

This means Christianity should influence our private and public lives.

A believer should be responsible in personal habits, fair in business dealings, respectful in relationships and faithful in spiritual commitments.

4. We must live with the expectation of Christ's return (verse 13).

Paul directs believers to look for the blessed hope and glorious appearing of Jesus Christ.

The return of Christ reminds Christians that life is more than present comfort, possessions and achievements.

Our conduct should be shaped by the reality that we will give account to God.

5. Christ redeemed us to become a purified people (verse 14).

Jesus gave Himself to redeem us from all iniquity and purify a people for His own possession, zealous of good works.

This is the purpose of salvation in practical terms: God is forming a people who belong to Him and demonstrate His character through their lives.

A Christian should therefore become increasingly committed to doing what is right.

D. Philippians 2:12–13 — Working Out What God Works In

Paul writes:

"Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling." — Philippians 2:12 KJV.

This verse is sometimes misunderstood as teaching that Christians must earn their salvation through personal effort.

However, verse 13 provides the necessary explanation:

"For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure."

1. Salvation must be worked out in daily living.

Paul is encouraging believers to demonstrate the reality of their salvation through practical obedience.

The expression "work out" does not mean "work for." It means allowing the salvation received through Christ to find expression in daily conduct.

For example, a person who has received Christ should increasingly show patience, truthfulness, forgiveness, responsibility and love.

2. Christian responsibility involves reverence and seriousness.

The expression "with fear and trembling" points to a reverent attitude towards God.

Believers must not treat spiritual matters carelessly.

We should take our conduct seriously because we belong to God and are accountable to Him.

3. God provides the power for obedience.

Verse 13 reminds us that God works in believers both to desire and to do what pleases Him.

This is a powerful balance.

Christian living requires personal responsibility, but it is not achieved through human strength alone.

We cooperate with God's work in us through faith, obedience, prayer, Scripture and dependence on the Holy Spirit.

THEOLOGICAL CLARIFICATION: AVOIDING EXTREMES

To understand salvation and grace correctly, believers must avoid the following errors.

1. Salvation cannot be earned through religious activities.

Church attendance, fasting, giving, humanitarian work and ministry service are important, but none of these can purchase salvation.

Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ.

2. Grace is not permission to continue in sin.

Romans 6:1–2 asks whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may abound. Paul's answer is emphatic: "God forbid."

Grace provides forgiveness and the power to live differently. It should never be used as an excuse for deliberate rebellion.

3. Good works are the evidence of salvation, not the price of salvation.

Ephesians 2:8–10 must be understood as one complete argument.

We are saved by grace, through faith, and created in Christ for good works.

4. Christian growth is a process.

Receiving salvation does not mean that a believer becomes instantly mature in every area.

Spiritual growth requires teaching, discipline, correction, accountability and dependence on the Holy Spirit.

5. God's grace does not remove human responsibility.

A Christian cannot deliberately neglect family, education, work, health or financial obligations and blame everything on God's sovereignty.

Believers are expected to be faithful stewards of the opportunities and responsibilities entrusted to them.

6. Forgiveness does not always remove earthly consequences.

A person who has committed a crime and genuinely repented may receive God's forgiveness, but this does not automatically cancel legal consequences or the need for restitution.

Grace does not destroy justice or responsibility.

7. Good works do not make us superior to others.

Our good conduct should produce humility and gratitude, not pride or condemnation of those who are still struggling.

We are all dependent on God's grace.

DOCTRINAL ALIGNMENT

This lesson agrees with the following biblical doctrines:

- Human sinfulness: All humanity has sinned and needs God's salvation (Romans 3:23).
- Salvation by grace: Salvation is God's gift received through faith, not human achievement (Ephesians 2:8–9).
- Justification by faith: Believers are declared righteous through faith in Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1).
- Redemption: Christ gave Himself to deliver humanity from sin (Titus 2:14).
- Sanctification: God's grace trains believers to reject ungodliness and live righteously (Titus 2:11–12).
- Christian responsibility: Genuine salvation should produce good works and practical obedience (Ephesians 2:10; James 2:17).
- Divine empowerment: God works in believers to enable them to desire and do His will (Philippians 2:13).
- Christian hope: Believers look forward to the glorious appearing of Jesus Christ (Titus 2:13).

KEY TRUTHS / LESSON HIGHLIGHTS

- Salvation is God's gift, not a reward for human performance.
- Every person needs salvation because of the reality of sin.
- Jesus Christ is the foundation and means of our salvation.
- Grace brings forgiveness, reconciliation and a new relationship with God.
- Grace does not encourage sin; it teaches us to reject ungodliness.
- Good works do not purchase salvation but demonstrate its transforming influence.
- Christian living requires personal discipline and dependence on the Holy Spirit.
- Believers must take responsibility for their conduct, families, work and service.
- The grace that saves us should also be visible in the way we treat others.

LIFE APPLICATION

How should the message of salvation and grace influence everyday living?

A. In personal character

A Christian who understands grace should not become careless about character.

The person should continually examine attitudes, habits, speech and behaviour.

If someone was previously known for anger, dishonesty or selfishness, the transforming work of grace should become increasingly visible.

B. In marriage and family life

A husband who has received God's grace should learn to demonstrate patience, love, faithfulness and responsibility.

A wife should also reflect grace through wisdom, respect, honesty and commitment.

Parents must understand that children are not merely their dependants but responsibilities entrusted to them by God.

Christian homes should become places where grace is practised through forgiveness, discipline, kindness and accountability.

C. In business and professional life

A Christian should not use God's grace to excuse corruption.

Grace should motivate fairness, diligence, honesty and respect for agreements.

An employer should pay workers fairly. An employee should perform assigned duties faithfully. A trader should avoid dishonest measurements and deceptive advertising.

D. In financial management

God's grace should influence how believers handle money.

Christians should learn budgeting, saving, generosity, responsible borrowing and avoidance of waste.

A believer should not become financially irresponsible while expecting God to continually solve preventable problems.

E. In relationships

People who understand grace should become more willing to forgive, apologise, show compassion and pursue reconciliation.

However, forgiveness does not mean remaining in an abusive or dangerous situation. Appropriate boundaries, protection and professional assistance may be necessary.

F. In church service

Ministry is a privilege and responsibility, not an opportunity for personal pride.

A person who has received grace should serve faithfully, respect others and avoid exploiting the church for personal gain.

G. In society

Christians should demonstrate the values of grace through compassion, justice, integrity and service.

Supporting vulnerable people, helping children access education, caring for the elderly, assisting people in correctional facilities and participating in community development are practical ways believers can demonstrate Christian responsibility.

H. In personal development

A Christian should not use salvation as an excuse for intellectual or professional laziness.

God's grace should motivate believers to develop their abilities, acquire useful skills, pursue excellence and become productive members of society.

CASE STUDY / REAL-LIFE SCENARIO

Case Study: The Church Member Who Misunderstood Grace

Brother Samuel has been a member of a local church for several years. He regularly attends services and contributes financially to church programmes.

However, his business practices are questionable. He sometimes gives customers false information, delays paying employees and manipulates financial records.

When a church leader confronts him, Samuel responds that nobody is perfect and that God is a God of grace. He argues that Christians are saved by faith, not by works, so people should not judge his behaviour.

Meanwhile, his wife complains that he neglects family responsibilities and frequently becomes aggressive when challenged.

Samuel believes that his religious activities and financial contributions should be enough to demonstrate his commitment to God.

Questions for Discussion:

- What misunderstanding of grace is evident in Samuel's attitude?
- How does Ephesians 2:8–10 correct his understanding?
- What does Titus 2:11–14 teach about the purpose of grace?
- Why are Samuel's financial contributions insufficient evidence of genuine Christian maturity?
- What practical steps should Samuel take to demonstrate repentance?
- How should church leaders correct members who misuse the doctrine of grace?
- What is the difference between condemning a person and holding that person accountable?

Teaching Insight:

Samuel has confused freedom from the penalty of sin with freedom to continue practising sin.

The grace of God does not encourage irresponsibility. It calls believers into transformation.

Samuel must acknowledge his wrongdoing, stop dishonest practices, make appropriate restitution, fulfil his family responsibilities and submit himself to biblical correction and accountability.

The church must show him grace while refusing to endorse behaviour that contradicts the gospel.

PERSONAL REFLECTION AND ACTION POINT

Take a few minutes to examine your understanding of salvation and grace.

- Do I understand that salvation is a gift of God's grace?
- Am I depending on religious activities rather than genuine faith in Christ?
- Are there sinful habits I continue to defend instead of surrendering to God?
- Does my conduct demonstrate gratitude for the salvation I have received?
- Am I responsible in my family, work, finances and relationships?
- Do I show the same grace to others that I expect God to show me?
- Is there an area where I need to apologise, make restitution or correct my behaviour?

Personal declaration:

I am saved by the grace of God through faith in Jesus Christ. I cannot earn salvation through my efforts, but I will not misuse God's grace. I am called to live a life of holiness, integrity, love and responsibility. God is working in me both to desire and to do His good pleasure. I will demonstrate the reality of my salvation through my character, relationships, work and service. By His grace, I will live a life that brings glory to Christ. Amen.

INVITATION TO SALVATION

Salvation is the greatest gift God offers humanity. It cannot be purchased with money, inherited through family background or obtained merely through church membership.

It is received through genuine repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.

If you have never surrendered your life to Jesus, or if you have been living in deliberate rebellion against God, today is an opportunity to respond to His grace.

Suggested prayer of commitment:

Heavenly Father, I come before You acknowledging that I am a sinner and cannot save myself. I believe that Jesus Christ died for my sins and rose again. I repent of my sins and place my faith in Him. Please forgive me, cleanse me and make me new. Teach me to live under Your grace and not misuse Your forgiveness. Give me the strength to walk in holiness, obedience and responsibility. Let my life bring honour to Your name. In Jesus' name, Amen.

This prayer is not a magic formula. Salvation is received through genuine repentance and personal faith in Jesus Christ.

ACTION POINT FOR THE WEEK

WEEKLY ASSIGNMENT

Every participant should complete the following exercises:

- Bible study: Read Ephesians 2:1–10 and write down five things God has done for believers through Christ.
- Personal examination: Identify one area where you have been using grace as an excuse for irresponsible behaviour. Decide on a practical change.
- Restitution and reconciliation: If you have wronged someone through dishonesty, neglect or injustice, take an appropriate step towards correction, apology or restitution where safe and possible.
- Demonstrate grace: Deliberately show kindness to someone who cannot repay you. This may involve helping a struggling neighbour, supporting a vulnerable person or encouraging someone who is discouraged.
- Personal discipline: Identify one responsibility you have been neglecting in your family, work, education, finances or spiritual life. Prepare a realistic plan to address it.

CLOSING PRAYER

Heavenly Father, we thank You for the gift of salvation through Jesus Christ. Thank You for loving us when we were helpless in sin and for extending Your grace and mercy to us.

Help us to understand the true meaning of grace. Deliver us from religious pride, spiritual laziness and every attempt to use Your forgiveness as an excuse for wrongdoing.

Let Your grace transform our hearts, renew our minds and guide our conduct. Teach us to become responsible in our families, honest in our businesses, faithful in our workplaces and compassionate towards people in need.

May our lives demonstrate the power of the gospel. Help us to grow in holiness, integrity and service until the return of our Lord Jesus Christ.

In Jesus' mighty name. Amen.

CONCLUSION

Salvation is God's gracious intervention in the life of humanity. Through Jesus Christ, we receive forgiveness, reconciliation, justification and a new relationship with God.

We do not earn this gift through religious activities or good works. We receive it through faith.

However, the grace that saves us also transforms us. It teaches us to reject ungodliness, practise righteousness and become people who are zealous for good works.

Christianity must therefore be understood as both a gift received and a life to be lived.

We must never confuse grace with permission to be irresponsible. Neither should we confuse good works with the price of salvation.

We are saved by grace, empowered by grace and called to demonstrate that grace through responsible Christian living.

Teacher's Final Emphasis: Never work to earn what Christ has freely given you. Instead, allow the salvation you have received to become visible in the way you live. Grace is not an excuse for irresponsibility; it is God's power and instruction for a transformed life.

lessons.conclusion:
Salvation is God's gracious intervention in the life of humanity. Through Jesus Christ, we receive forgiveness, reconciliation, justification and a new relationship with God.

We do not earn this gift through religious activities or good works. We receive it through faith.

However, the grace that saves us also transforms us. It teaches us to reject ungodliness, practise righteousness and become people who are zealous for good works.

Christianity must therefore be understood as both a gift received and a life to be lived.

We must never confuse grace with permission to be irresponsible. Neither should we confuse good works with the price of salvation.

We are saved by grace, empowered by grace and called to demonstrate that grace through responsible Christian living.

lessons.title: LESSON 6 — DEVELOPING A CONSISTENT AND INTIMATE RELATIONSHIP WITH GOD
lessons.theme: Developing a consistent and intimate relationship with God
lessons.memoryVerse: John 15:5 (KJV): “I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.”
lessons.introduction:
One of the greatest challenges facing contemporary Christianity is the difference between being religious and genuinely knowing God.

Many people attend church regularly, participate in Christian activities, hold leadership positions, sing in choirs, preach sermons, and even occupy prominent positions in Christian organisations. Yet, beneath these activities, some struggle to maintain a consistent personal relationship with God.

It is possible to be busy with the things of God while gradually becoming distant from God Himself.

A person may know several Bible passages without allowing the Word to transform their character. Someone may lead prayers publicly but struggle to maintain a private prayer life. Another person may be actively involved in ministry but have little time for personal fellowship with the Lord.

This reveals an important truth: Spiritual activity is not necessarily evidence of spiritual intimacy.

Developing an intimate relationship with God requires more than occasional religious enthusiasm. It involves knowing Him personally, loving Him sincerely, trusting His character, obeying His Word, and making Him central to everyday decisions.

Consider a marriage relationship. A husband and wife cannot maintain intimacy simply because they live in the same house. They must communicate, spend time together, demonstrate love, resolve misunderstandings, and remain committed to one another.

Likewise, our relationship with God must be cultivated. Salvation establishes our relationship with Him through Christ, but our experience of fellowship and spiritual maturity develops as we continue walking with Him.

The question we must honestly answer is:

If all our church activities were suspended for one month, would our personal relationship with God remain strong?

This lesson challenges us to move beyond occasional encounters with God into a consistent lifestyle of fellowship with Him.

DATE: Sunday, February 7, 2027.

CENTRAL TEACHING: Christianity is not merely participation in religious activities but a living, growing, and intimate relationship with God, sustained through fellowship, obedience, prayer, worship, the Word, and daily dependence on the Holy Spirit.

D. BIBLICAL EXPLANATION: WHAT THE TEXTS MEAN

1. JOHN 15:1–11 — ABIDING IN CHRIST AS THE FOUNDATION OF INTIMACY

Jesus presents Himself as the true vine and believers as the branches. This illustration provides one of the clearest biblical explanations of our relationship with Christ.

A branch does not produce fruit independently. Its life, nourishment, and productivity depend on its connection to the vine. Once disconnected, it loses the source of its nourishment and eventually becomes unproductive.

Jesus teaches that the believer's spiritual productivity depends on remaining connected to Him.

a. Christ is the source of spiritual life (John 15:1).

Jesus identifies Himself as the true vine. This means that genuine spiritual life originates from Him. Our strength, spiritual growth, character transformation, and capacity for fruitful service cannot be sustained independently of Christ. A Christian who attempts to live by personal strength alone will eventually discover the limitations of human ability.

b. God expects spiritual fruitfulness (John 15:2).

The Father is described as the husbandman who tends the vine. The pruning process represents God's work of removing things that hinder spiritual growth and increasing fruitfulness.

Sometimes God uses His Word, correction, discipline, life experiences, and conviction by the Holy Spirit to deal with attitudes and habits that are inconsistent with His purpose.

Not every uncomfortable experience means God is punishing us. Sometimes spiritual development requires correction, adjustment, and the removal of unhealthy attachments.

c. Abiding in Christ requires continuous dependence (John 15:4–5).

The word abide communicates the idea of remaining, continuing, and dwelling. Intimacy with God is not an occasional experience reserved for Sunday services, prayer meetings, or special spiritual programmes. It is a daily relationship.

A believer who prays only when facing difficulties has not yet developed the discipline of consistent fellowship. God wants us to involve Him in our decisions, relationships, work, family responsibilities, challenges, and everyday activities.

d. God's Word sustains our relationship with Him (John 15:7).

Jesus connects abiding in Him with allowing His words to abide in us. This means that intimacy with God cannot be separated from Scripture.

We cannot claim to be growing closer to God while consistently ignoring what He has revealed about His character, will, and expectations. The Word corrects our thinking, strengthens our faith, and guides our decisions.

e. Obedience is evidence of love (John 15:10).

Jesus connects abiding in His love with keeping His commandments. True intimacy is not merely emotional excitement during worship. It produces a lifestyle that honours God.

A person cannot continually embrace disobedience and expect to enjoy healthy fellowship with God.

f. Intimacy produces joy and fruitfulness (John 15:11).

Jesus explains that His teachings are intended to produce fullness of joy in His followers. Therefore, intimacy with God is not a burden or an unnecessary religious demand. It is the foundation of a meaningful and spiritually fruitful life.

2. PSALM 63:1–8 — DEVELOPING A DEEP HUNGER FOR GOD

Psalm 63 reveals David's personal longing for God while he was in the wilderness of Judah. David was experiencing a difficult environment, yet his greatest concern was not merely his physical comfort. His heart longed for God's presence.

a. Intimacy begins with a genuine hunger for God (Psalm 63:1).

David declares that his soul thirsts for God. Physical hunger reminds us of our dependence on food, while spiritual hunger reveals our awareness of our dependence on God.

A believer who has no desire for prayer, Scripture, worship, or fellowship should examine the condition of their spiritual appetite. Sometimes our spiritual hunger becomes weak because we have allowed other interests to occupy the place that belongs to God.

b. God's presence is more valuable than outward prosperity (Psalm 63:2–3).

David remembers God's power and glory and declares that God's lovingkindness is better than life. This is a remarkable declaration.

Many people measure God's goodness by financial success, physical comfort, recognition, and material possessions. David demonstrates that God's presence is more valuable than all these things.

A person may possess wealth and still experience spiritual emptiness. Another may face difficult circumstances yet enjoy deep satisfaction because of their relationship with God.

c. Intimacy involves personal worship (Psalm 63:4–5).

David speaks about blessing God, lifting his hands, and praising Him. Worship is not restricted to singing in church. It is a personal expression of love, reverence, gratitude, and submission to God.

A believer should learn to worship God privately, even when there is no musical instrument, choir, congregation, or special atmosphere.

d. Consistent fellowship requires intentional attention (Psalm 63:6).

David remembers God upon his bed and meditates on Him during the night watches. This demonstrates that fellowship with God should not be restricted to convenient moments.

Even in quiet moments, during work breaks, while travelling, or before sleeping, believers can direct their thoughts towards God. This does not mean neglecting responsibilities. Rather, it means developing an awareness of God that influences our entire daily lives.

e. Intimacy produces confidence in God's protection (Psalm 63:7–8).

David describes God as his help and declares that his soul follows closely after Him. His confidence is rooted in God's character, not in the absence of difficulties.

A person who genuinely knows God develops the confidence to remain faithful even when circumstances are uncertain.

3. JAMES 4:7–10 — THE RESPONSIBILITY OF PURSUING INTIMACY WITH GOD

James addresses believers whose lives were being affected by worldly desires, pride, selfish ambitions, and conflicts. He presents practical instructions for restoring a healthy relationship with God.

a. Submit yourselves to God (James 4:7).

Submission means recognising God's authority and willingly placing our desires, plans, ambitions, and decisions under His leadership.

Some people want God's blessings without submitting to His instructions. They want Him to support their plans but are unwilling to allow Him to correct those plans. Intimacy requires surrender.

b. Resist the devil (James 4:7).

A consistent relationship with God requires spiritual alertness. Believers must resist temptation, deception, ungodly influences, and every practice that seeks to weaken their obedience to God.

We cannot deliberately entertain what destroys our spiritual lives and expect to remain spiritually healthy.

c. Draw near to God (James 4:8).

This is one of the most direct biblical invitations to intimacy. God invites His people to approach Him.

Drawing near involves prayer, worship, repentance, studying Scripture, obedience, and deliberate fellowship. The promise that God will draw near to us reveals His willingness to receive those who sincerely seek Him.

d. Cleanse your hands and purify your hearts (James 4:8).

James addresses both outward behaviour and inward motives. Clean hands point towards the need for righteous conduct, while pure hearts point towards sincerity and inner transformation.

A person may appear spiritually committed publicly while secretly entertaining bitterness, dishonesty, sexual immorality, greed, jealousy, or pride. God desires integrity both inside and outside.

e. Humble yourselves before the Lord (James 4:9–10).

Humility involves acknowledging our dependence on God, recognising our failures, and remaining teachable. Pride makes people resistant to correction, but humility creates room for spiritual growth. God promises to lift up those who humble themselves before Him.

4. PHILIPPIANS 3:7–14 — MAKING THE KNOWLEDGE OF CHRIST OUR GREATEST PURSUIT

Paul's testimony in this passage reveals a man whose priorities had been radically transformed by his encounter with Christ. Before his conversion, Paul had significant religious credentials, achievements, and recognition. However, after encountering Christ, he began to evaluate everything differently.

a. Knowing Christ is more valuable than worldly achievements (Philippians 3:7–8).

Paul considers his former gains as loss compared with the surpassing value of knowing Christ. This does not mean education, professional development, financial stability, or personal achievements are inherently wrong.

Rather, none of these things should compete with Christ for the highest place in our lives. A person can become so committed to career advancement, business expansion, social recognition, or ministry popularity that personal fellowship with God gradually suffers.

b. Intimacy with Christ involves trusting His righteousness (Philippians 3:9).

Paul recognises that righteousness does not come from human achievement or religious performance but through faith in Christ.

Our relationship with God is founded on grace, not on our ability to impress Him. Spiritual disciplines do not purchase God's love. They help us cultivate fellowship with the God who has already brought us into relationship with Himself through Christ.

c. Knowing Christ includes experiencing His power (Philippians 3:10).

Paul expresses his desire to know Christ, the power of His resurrection, and the fellowship of His sufferings. Knowing Christ is more than knowing information about Him.

It involves experiencing His transforming power, sharing in His values, and remaining faithful even when obedience becomes costly.

d. Spiritual maturity requires continuous growth (Philippians 3:12).

Paul acknowledges that he has not yet attained perfection. This is important because some believers become spiritually complacent after years of Christian experience.

They assume that because they have been Christians for a long time, they have automatically become mature. Paul demonstrates that spiritual maturity includes recognising how much growth is still needed.

e. Intimacy requires intentional pursuit (Philippians 3:13–14).

Paul describes his determination to forget what is behind and press towards what lies ahead. Developing intimacy with God requires intentional effort.

Past spiritual experiences are valuable, but yesterday's prayer life cannot replace today's fellowship with God. We must continue pursuing Him.

E. THEOLOGICAL CLARIFICATION: AVOIDING EXTREMES

Developing intimacy with God requires biblical balance. Some misunderstandings can create unhealthy expectations about Christian fellowship.

1. Intimacy is not the same as emotional excitement.

A person may experience strong emotions during worship and still struggle with obedience. Emotions can accompany genuine fellowship, but they are not the ultimate measure of spiritual maturity. A consistent relationship with God is demonstrated through faith, obedience, love, and perseverance.

2. Intimacy does not mean God will always communicate through audible voices.

God has revealed Himself through Scripture, and the Holy Spirit works in believers to guide, convict, teach, and transform them. We must not measure our relationship with God by whether we hear an audible voice. Every perceived spiritual impression must be tested against the authority of Scripture.

3. Spiritual disciplines do not earn salvation or God's favour.

Prayer, fasting, Bible study, worship, and meditation are important, but they are not payments through which we purchase God's love. Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9). Spiritual disciplines are responses to God's grace and means of cultivating fellowship with Him.

4. Intimacy does not mean a believer will never experience difficulties.

David experienced wilderness seasons. Paul experienced suffering. Jesus Himself faced opposition. A close relationship with God does not eliminate every challenge. It provides spiritual strength, perspective, and confidence to remain faithful through challenges.

5. Intimacy must produce transformation.

A person cannot consistently claim closeness to God while deliberately refusing His instructions. Genuine fellowship should progressively influence our character, speech, relationships, priorities, and conduct.

F. DOCTRINAL ALIGNMENT

1. The Doctrine of Salvation: Our relationship with God is established through Jesus Christ, not through human merit (Romans 5:1–2).
2. The Doctrine of the Holy Spirit: The Holy Spirit helps believers grow in fellowship, understanding, holiness, and spiritual maturity (Romans 8:14–16).
3. The Doctrine of Sanctification: God desires continuous transformation in the lives of His children (1 Thessalonians 4:3).
4. The Doctrine of the Word of God: Scripture provides the foundation for knowing God's will and living a life that pleases Him (2 Timothy 3:16–17).
5. The Doctrine of Christian Perseverance: Believers are called to continue in faith and remain steadfast in Christ (Colossians 2:6–7).
6. The Doctrine of Prayer and Fellowship: Believers are invited to approach God confidently through Christ (Hebrews 4:16).

Central Doctrinal Truth: A genuine relationship with God begins through faith in Jesus Christ and develops through continuous fellowship, dependence, obedience, and the transforming work of the Holy Spirit.

G. KEY TRUTHS AND LESSON HIGHLIGHTS

1. Christianity is fundamentally a relationship with God, not merely participation in religious activities.
2. Jesus Christ is the source of our spiritual life and fruitfulness.
3. Consistent intimacy requires daily fellowship rather than occasional spiritual excitement.
4. God's Word is essential for knowing His character and understanding His will.
5. A genuine hunger for God must be deliberately cultivated.
6. Obedience is an important expression of love for God.
7. Humility and repentance help restore healthy fellowship with God.
8. Spiritual maturity requires continuous growth and intentional pursuit.
9. God desires inward transformation, not merely outward religious performance.
10. The ultimate goal of intimacy is to know Christ more deeply and become increasingly conformed to His character.

H. LIFE APPLICATION

The knowledge of intimacy with God becomes meaningful when it influences our everyday decisions.

1. The busy Christian

A businessperson wakes up early, rushes to work, attends meetings, handles financial transactions, and returns home exhausted. Prayer and Bible study are repeatedly postponed until there is no time left. After several months, the individual discovers that business activities have gradually replaced personal fellowship with God.

The lesson is that busyness should not become an excuse for spiritual neglect. We must deliberately create time for God.

2. The minister who has neglected personal fellowship

A minister spends several hours preparing sermons, counselling members, attending meetings, and organising programmes. However, personal prayer has become irregular. The minister is constantly speaking to people about God but rarely spending personal time with God.

Ministry responsibility must never replace personal intimacy with the Lord.

3. The believer facing disappointment

A Christian prays for a particular breakthrough, but the expected answer does not come immediately. The person becomes discouraged and begins withdrawing from prayer.

Psalm 63 teaches us that our desire for God must be deeper than our desire for favourable circumstances. We must learn to seek God because of who He is, not only because of what we expect Him to do.

4. The young believer influenced by social media

A young Christian spends hours consuming online content but struggles to devote fifteen minutes to Scripture and prayer. Gradually, worldly opinions begin to shape the person's values more than God's Word.

This individual needs to recognise the importance of spiritual discipline and carefully evaluate what receives attention every day.

Practical steps towards developing intimacy with God:
- Establish a definite daily time for personal fellowship.
- Read Scripture consistently and meditate on its meaning.
- Maintain a prayer life that includes thanksgiving, confession, intercession, and personal communion.
- Practise obedience even when it is inconvenient.
- Remove habits and relationships that consistently weaken spiritual commitment.
- Develop a lifestyle of worship and gratitude.
- Examine your motives regularly.
- Remain connected to a healthy Christian community.
- Seek God's guidance before making major decisions.
- Continue pursuing spiritual growth regardless of how long you have been a Christian.

J. CASE STUDY / REAL-LIFE SCENARIO

Case Study: The Active but Spiritually Empty Christian

Daniel has been a Christian for twelve years. He is actively involved in church activities, attends Sunday services, participates in evangelism, and occasionally leads prayer meetings. He is respected by many church members because of his commitment to ministry.

However, Daniel has developed a habit of neglecting personal prayer and Bible study. He only prays seriously when he faces financial difficulties, sickness, or family problems.

Recently, he has become impatient, easily offended, and increasingly dependent on his own judgement. He knows many Bible passages but rarely reflects on how they should influence his personal conduct.

One day, a younger Christian asks him: “Sir, you always encourage us to spend time with God. How is your own personal relationship with God?”

Daniel becomes uncomfortable because he realises that his public Christian activities have not been matched by consistent private fellowship.

Questions for Reflection:
1. What is the major spiritual problem in Daniel's life?
2. Is Daniel's involvement in church activities necessarily evidence of spiritual intimacy? Explain.
3. Which of the four Bible passages studied in this lesson speaks most directly to his situation?
4. What practical steps should Daniel take to restore consistency in his fellowship with God?
5. What lessons can church leaders and other believers learn from Daniel's experience?

Teaching Point: Never allow public ministry to become a substitute for private fellowship with God. What we do for God must flow from our relationship with Him.

K. PERSONAL REFLECTION AND ACTION POINT

Personal Reflection Questions:
1. When last did I spend meaningful time with God without rushing?
2. Do I study the Bible to know God and obey Him, or merely to prepare sermons, teachings, and religious discussions?
3. Is my prayer life consistent or dependent on emergencies?
4. Are there habits, relationships, ambitions, or distractions competing with my relationship with God?
5. Am I becoming more loving, patient, humble, obedient, and Christlike?
6. If someone examined my private life, would there be evidence of my public confession of faith?

Personal Declaration:
“I will not be satisfied with merely knowing about God. I desire to know Him personally and walk with Him consistently. I will make room for His Word, prayer, worship, obedience, and the leading of the Holy Spirit. My relationship with Christ will remain my highest priority. I will continue to grow in grace and in the knowledge of my Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ. Amen.”

L. ACTION POINT FOR THE WEEK

Seven-Day Personal Intimacy Challenge

Monday: Spend at least 20 minutes in personal prayer and read John 15:1–5.
Tuesday: Read Psalm 63:1–8 and write down three things that increase your hunger for God.
Wednesday: Read James 4:7–10 and identify one area where you need to surrender to God.
Thursday: Read Philippians 3:7–14 and examine your priorities.
Friday: Spend time in thanksgiving and worship without making requests.
Saturday: Practise intentional obedience in one area where you have been struggling.
Sunday: Review your spiritual progress and write down what you have learnt about your relationship with God.

Weekly Assignment:

Each participant should write a one-page personal reflection titled: “MY CURRENT RELATIONSHIP WITH GOD AND THE CHANGES I MUST MAKE.”

The reflection should identify at least three areas of improvement and practical steps towards developing a more consistent relationship with God.

M. CLOSING PRAYER

1. Father, give me a deeper hunger and thirst for Your presence, in Jesus' name.
2. Lord, deliver me from every distraction that competes with my relationship with You.
3. Holy Spirit, help me develop a consistent and disciplined prayer life.
4. Father, let Your Word dwell richly in my heart and transform my thoughts, decisions, and character.
5. Lord, remove every attitude of pride, disobedience, spiritual laziness, and complacency from my life.
6. Father, help me to remain in Christ and produce lasting spiritual fruit.
7. Lord, let my private relationship with You become stronger than my public religious activities.
8. Father, give me the grace to pursue You faithfully in every season of my life.

In Jesus' mighty name. Amen.

N. CONCLUSION

Developing a consistent and intimate relationship with God is not an optional responsibility for a believer. It is fundamental to Christian living.

Jesus teaches us that without Him we can do nothing. David demonstrates that our souls must genuinely hunger for God's presence. James reminds us that drawing near to God requires submission, humility, and repentance. Paul shows us that knowing Christ is more valuable than worldly achievements and that spiritual maturity requires continuous pursuit.

The greatest tragedy in Christianity is not necessarily the absence of religious activities but the possibility of becoming so occupied with religious activities that we neglect the God we claim to serve.

God is not simply interested in what we do in His name. He desires that we know Him, love Him, obey Him, and walk with Him.

Remember: The strength of your public Christian life is sustained by the depth and consistency of your private relationship with God.

Let us therefore move beyond occasional encounters and develop a lifelong relationship of intimacy with our Heavenly Father through Jesus Christ.

FINAL CHALLENGE:

Do not merely seek God's hand for what He can give you. Seek His face because of who He is. Let knowing Christ become your greatest pursuit.

lessons.theme: Understanding prayer: Principles, power and practice
lessons.memoryVerse: Philippians 4:6 (KJV): “Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.”
lessons.introduction:
Prayer is one of the most important practices in the Christian faith, yet it is also one of the most misunderstood.

Some Christians consider prayer primarily as a means of asking God for material blessings, protection, healing, financial breakthroughs, or solutions to personal problems. Others approach prayer as a religious obligation, something they must perform because they are Christians.

While prayer certainly includes making requests to God, its meaning is much deeper than presenting needs before Him.

Prayer is communication and fellowship with God. It is the believer's expression of dependence, worship, gratitude, submission, confession, and confidence in the Father through Jesus Christ.

Consider a child who only communicates with a parent whenever money, food, or assistance is needed. Although the child may have a genuine relationship with the parent, the communication is incomplete because it is centred almost entirely on personal needs.

Unfortunately, some believers approach God in a similar manner. They remember Him during emergencies but neglect fellowship when everything appears to be going well.

Biblical prayer goes beyond emergencies. It is a lifestyle of continuous dependence on God.

Jesus did not merely instruct His disciples to pray; He taught them how to pray. When His disciples asked Him to teach them to pray, He provided a pattern that addresses God's honour, His kingdom, daily provision, forgiveness, spiritual protection, and deliverance from evil.

This demonstrates that prayer must be understood biblically rather than shaped by popular religious practices, emotional excitement, or human assumptions.

A believer must understand not only how to pray but also why prayer matters, what should characterise prayer, and how to approach God according to His revealed will.

Central Question: Are we praying merely to get things from God, or are we learning to relate with God, understand His will, and participate in His purposes through prayer?
